item.title: IDEA: eSIM Cards Explained: How They Work and How to Use Them Abroad
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Arriving in another country often comes with a familiar list of tasks: find the train platform, check the hotel address, message someone at home, and figure out whether your phone can get online. Mobile data makes these jobs easier, but choosing how to connect can be confusing. An eSIM lets you arrange mobile service without inserting another plastic SIM card into your phone. For travelers, students, and people working away from home, that removes one more errand from an already busy day. However, the technology and the plan are different. Having an eSIM does not automatically mean unlimited data, worldwide coverage, or free international calls. Understanding that distinction helps you choose a service that fits your device, destination, and routine. What Is an eSIM Card? An eSIM is a digital alternative to a removable SIM card. On compatible devices, built-in SIM hardware can securely hold an operator's downloadable profile. That profile allows the device to register with the mobile network and use the services included in a subscription or prepaid plan. If you are asking what is an eSIM card, the practical answer is that it does the familiar job of a SIM without requiring you to insert a separate card. Instead, you download the provider's profile. The word "card" can be misleading. Buying a travel eSIM usually means purchasing a digital service rather than receiving something in the post. Depending on the provider, you may install it through an app, a QR code, or your phone's built-in setup options. It is useful to separate the eSIM profile from the data package. Some services let you keep an installed profile and purchase additional packages later. Others may require a different installation process for new purchases. How Does an eSIM Work? A physical SIM contains information that identifies a mobile subscription to a network. An eSIM profile provides that information digitally. After installation and activation, your phone connects through the networks available to that provider in your location. The experience then feels much like using a conventional mobile plan. You open maps, browse websites, send messages, or join a video call through your apps. What changes is how you obtain and manage the connection. Installation and plan activation are not always the same. A provider might let you install a profile before departure but start the package's validity later. Another plan might begin its countdown at purchase or installation. Always read activation conditions before preparing your phone for a trip. An eSIM also needs network coverage. It cannot create a signal in an underground tunnel, remote valley, or building where the network doesn't reach. eSIM vs Physical SIM: What Changes? Both formats can provide mobile connectivity. The main differences concern setup, device support, and how easily you can change services. Neither format guarantees better reception. An eSIM package on one network may perform differently from a physical SIM on another. That difference comes from the service and local conditions, not due to the absence of plastic. How to Check Whether Your Phone Supports eSIM Before buying, check your exact phone model and the country or region where it was sold. Similar-looking versions of a handset can have different SIM capabilities. A useful first check is to open the phone's dial pad and enter *#06#. On many compatible smartphones, the information displayed includes an EID, the identifier linked to the device's eSIM hardware. Seeing an EID is a good sign that the phone supports eSIM. If it does not appear, check device information in Settings and consult the manufacturer's documentation. Do not rely on the dial-pad result alone to decide if a provider will work. Also check these three points: - Carrier lock: Your phone generally needs to be unlocked to use a different provider's travel eSIM. - Provider support: Confirm your exact device against the service's compatibility information. - Software: Complete any required system updates before installation. On an iPhone, the lock status is available under Settings > General> About. "No SIM restrictions" indicates an unlocked device. Android menus vary, so ask your current carrier if the status is unclear. Installing a profile while you have a reliable internet connection gives you time to follow instructions carefully. It also reduces the need to find a mobile shop immediately after landing. Keep the purchase confirmation and setup guidance accessible offline. If a QR code is involved, check whether your device can import it from an image or if you need to display it on another screen. A city break and a month of remote work create different demands. Someone using maps and messaging may need less data than someone uploading videos or regularly sharing data with a laptop. Country-specific, regional, and global packages suit different routes. Check the destination list, including stopovers where you expect to need mobile data. A regional label alone does not show everything included. On supported dual-SIM phones, you may be able to retain your home line while selecting the travel eSIM for mobile data. This can help you keep access to your regular number during a trip. Leaving that line switched on does not make its calls or messages free. Check your home carrier's roaming charges and settings, especially if you plan to answer calls abroad. A prepaid allowance gives you a set amount of data for a stated period. That can make budgeting easier if you understand expiry dates, top-up options, and recurring payments. Compare it with your existing plan before purchasing. Your home subscription may already include roaming benefits for the destination. Preparing your mobile connection before departure can make arrival-day tasks easier. Understanding eSIM Profiles and Cross-Border Travel A border crossing does not always mean installing another profile. Some international services let you reuse the same profile and buy the appropriate package for the next destination. Ubigi is one example. It is provided by Transatel, an NTT company, and offers connectivity across more than 200 destinations through its reusable eSIM. Travelers can retain the profile rather than installing a fresh one for every supported destination. That does not mean a single purchased package includes all those destinations. The installed profile lets you access the service; the selected package determines where your allowance applies, how much data you get, and how long it remains valid. For a trip involving several countries, write down the full route before choosing a package. Compare a regional plan with separate country packages, considering cost and convenience of managing them. Tethering turns a phone's mobile data connection into an internet connection for another device, commonly through a password-protected Wi-Fi hotspot. It can be useful when a laptop needs connectivity, and the available Wi-Fi is inconvenient or unreliable. Hotspot rules vary between services, so check them before buying. Ubigi allows tethering, making connection sharing a practical option for travelers carrying several devices. Shared devices use the same data allowance. A laptop can consume it quickly through software updates, cloud backups, or large downloads. Before connecting, pause automatic updates and check which applications run in the background. Use a strong hotspot password, and turn off sharing when you're done. Also plan for battery use: a phone supplying data to other devices may need charging sooner. For important meetings, have a second connection option available if possible. The screens differ between phones and providers, but the preparation follows a straightforward sequence. 1. Confirm compatibility and unlocking. Check eSIM support, carrier lock status, and the provider's device requirements. Do this before paying for a package. 2. Read the package details. Confirm destination coverage, data allowance, validity, activation rules, and hotspot permissions. Check whether the service is data-only or includes a phone number, calls, and SMS. 3. Purchase through the official service. Use the provider's official site or app. For example, Ubigi's website purchase process provides an installation QR code by email. Its app also supports purchasing a package and following an in-app installation process. 4. Install with an internet connection. Follow the supplied instructions and give the new line an easy-to-recognize name, such as "Travel Data." Keep the profile installed unless the provider tells you otherwise. 5. Select the correct data line. At the destination, enable the travel profile and select it for mobile data. Enable data roaming on that line if the provider requires it. Review the home line separately and turn off automatic data switching where necessary to avoid unintended home-carrier data use. 6. Check the connection. Open a simple webpage or map. If it doesn't load, check the selected data line, package status, and the provider's troubleshooting instructions. Avoid deleting the profile as a first troubleshooting step, because reinstalling may require assistance. What to Check Before Buying an eSIM Plan A low advertised price is only useful when the package meets your needs. Compare the following details: Coverage: Check which destinations and local networks the plan includes. If your trip takes you beyond major cities, check coverage at each stop on your route. For example, if you're island-hopping in Greece, check each island you'll visit before buying a plan. Validity: Match the package to your dates and understand when the countdown starts. Buying early should not shorten the usable period. Data allowance: Review your phone's usage statistics as a starting point. Consider additional needs such as navigation, uploads, or laptop tethering. Speed conditions: Read fair-use terms, especially for packages described as unlimited. Check whether usage thresholds affect speed or hotspot access. Calls and messages: A data-only package supports internet apps but doesn't automatically provide a local number or SMS service. Support and top-ups: Find out how to contact support and whether you can add data without replacing the profile. Save key help information before departure. One mistake is assuming every modern smartphone supports every eSIM service. Exact model variants, carrier restrictions, and provider requirements still matter. Another is treating installation as proof that a package is active and ready everywhere. Check the destination, start conditions, and selected mobile data line separately. Travelers also underestimate background usage. Photo syncing, app downloads, and video autoplay can use data without being the main reason you use your phone. Adjust those settings before relying on a limited allowance. Finally, don't erase the travel profile just because the package expired. With reusable services, keeping the profile may make future purchases easier. Check the provider's instructions before deleting it or moving to a new phone. Can an eSIM work without Wi-Fi? Once installed and active, it provides mobile connectivity without Wi-Fi wherever the included network service is available. Initial installation generally requires an internet connection, so prepare ahead. Will an eSIM change my WhatsApp number? Using another line for mobile data does not require changing your WhatsApp number. Keep your existing account registration unless you intend to change it, and maintain a way to complete future account verification. Can I use an eSIM and a physical SIM together? Yes, on phones that support this combination. The number of profiles you can store and lines you can use simultaneously depend on the device. Is an eSIM always cheaper than roaming? No. Compare the full package cost with your carrier's roaming or travel passes. Your itinerary and usage determine which option offers better value. The most useful eSIM works with your phone and covers the places you need. Start with compatibility, then compare coverage, validity, data allowances, and connection-sharing rules. Set up the profile before you leave. Check the settings on arrival and track usage during the trip. Those practical steps matter more than choosing the biggest allowance or the most eye-catching offer. With the right package and a little preparation, mobile connectivity becomes one less thing to organize when you reach your destination. This story was published in partnership with Ubigi.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to save on a cruise: 35 money-saving tips from an expert cruiser
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Cruises can be truly affordable vacations — but that doesn’t mean you won’t run up a significant bill booking your sailing or spending during your trip. It’s also easy to overspend on certain travel costs when you don’t know all the best money-saving tricks. As someone who cruises often, I don’t have a huge budget to spend on onboard purchases for each sailing, so I’ve had to get wise on how to save money on a cruise. Some of my strategies are obvious and others I’ve learned from trial and error over more than 80 sailings. I’m happy to share the wealth, so to speak, so you can avoid money mistakes and stretch your travel budget as far as it can possibly go. Here are my 35 top tips on how to save on a cruise. How to save money on your cruise booking Book early. Most cruise lines increase prices as ships sell out. Book early to get the lowest prices, as well as the widest choice of cabin types and locations, plus dining times. Book at the last minute. The corollary advice is that cruise lines will sometimes drop prices or offer value-added promotions on cruises that have too many available cabins left a few months before their scheduled departures. You can find cheap deals on last-minute sailings, especially if you’re not picky about which cabin you get. Start looking about 90 days out for most big-ship sailings. Book a shoulder-season sailing. Spring and fall tend to be less busy travel times, and cruises during these shoulder-season months are priced accordingly. Pick a cruise at the beginning or end of the Alaska or Mediterranean season when the weather isn’t as optimal, and you’ll save big over the peak midseason voyages. Sailings departing after Thanksgiving but before Christmas are also less popular and, therefore, cheaper. Book an inside cabin. The cheapest room on the ship is an inside cabin, so choose one of those rooms if you want to spend less on your next sailing. You’ll get access to the same pools, restaurants, shows and activities as the folks in the balcony cabins; all you’re missing out on is a window and some more floor space. Some people actually prefer inside cabins for amazing sleep in the pitch dark or because they spend all their time out and about on the ship and are never in their room. Be flexible on dates. Many unpredictable factors combine to make one sailing more expensive than the identical itinerary the week before or after. If you can be flexible on which week you cruise, you can save money by choosing whichever sail date is cheaper. Book an older ship. Newer ships with their one-of-a-kind attractions and up-to-date everything get all the attention — and can command the highest prices. Seek out older ships to get a better cruise deal. Cruise lines maintain their older ships and often give them massive makeovers to add the latest restaurants and top-deck attractions, so you’ll hardly notice you’re on a 20-year-old ship. But your budget will notice the more affordable rates, leaving money in your pocket to spend on splurges like spa treatments and specialty dining. Look for sales and promotions. Cruise lines run sales so often that you’re wasting money if you book when there isn’t a deal. Some promotions are all about lower fares, while others save you money with included perks, like free Wi-Fi or a complimentary beverage package. Solo travelers should look out for sales that waive the single supplement, saving you up to 50% of the normal single cabin price. Families should watch out for kids-cruise-free sales or other discounted third- and fourth-guest offers. How do you find out about your favorite cruise line’s latest sales? Sign up for the brand’s email list or a large online travel agent’s deal alert newsletter, and they’ll send info on promos straight to your inbox. Check for price drops. If you book a cruise and discover that the price has decreased down the road, your cruise line or travel agent will often be able to issue you a price adjustment. Some passengers have even reported receiving more than one adjustment if the prices fall repeatedly. The key is to make sure you spot the lower prices before the final payment deadline passes. After that, the best a cruise line can usually do for your is to offer a cabin upgrade. Leverage your casino play. Cruise lines love casino players because they spend money on board. Once you’ve established yourself as a member of a cruise line’s players club, you might find yourself the recipient of cruise discounts and complimentary casino cruise offers. You can definitely save on a cruise when all you have to pay are taxes and fees. Be loyal to one cruise line. Sail once with a cruise line, and you’re eligible to join its loyalty program. All members are eligible for select past-passenger cruise fare discounts, but the most loyal members can access free upgrades or even free cruises. Request your shareholder credit. Cruisers who own 100 shares or more of the big three publicly traded cruise corporations — Carnival Corp., Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings and Royal Caribbean Group — can request onboard credit as a perk of being a shareholder. You can request it via an online form on each cruise line's website; the amount you'll receive, if approved, depends on the type of cruise you book. Credit can only be requested on full-fare voyages, and only one shareholder credit is permitted per stateroom. Choose a drive-to port. Parking a car for a week is almost guaranteed to be cheaper than airport transfers, flights and a precruise hotel for a family of four. Cruise ships depart from ports all along the U.S. and Canada coastlines; consider choosing a cruise that departs from a port within driving distance of your home to save money on your next cruise. Use a credit card that gives you perks. Even if your cruise fare isn't dirt cheap, you can still get more value from your vacation dollars when you pay for that vacation at sea with the right card. For example, book with The Platinum Card® from American Express, and its Cruise Privileges Program will get you double Membership Rewards points, onboard credit and cruise line-specific perks. Book a Carnival cruise with the Carnival Rewards™ Mastercard®, and you can earn extra Carnival Rewards points that you can redeem for cruise-related purchases and Loyalty Status stars that will fast track your elite status. Or, perhaps you can use your cruise final payment to make the minimum spending requirement on a new credit card and get a slew of points or miles you can use for a free trip down the road. Bid for an upgrade. Several major cruise lines, like Norwegian Cruise Line and MSC Cruises, offer select guests the option to bid for an upgraded cabin. Bid less than the difference between your cabin cost and the price of the nicer room, and if your bid is approved, you’ll get upgraded onboard digs at a discount. Use a travel agent. Most travel agents won’t charge you to use their cruise-booking services, but they can help you find the best deal on the best sailing for you, and they might even throw in a free bottle of Champagne or some onboard credit. If nothing else, these knowledgeable advisers can save you from making costly mistakes on the wrong cruise purchases, and that is a value in and of itself. Book your next cruise on board. Most cruise lines run a future cruise sales desk on board ships. If you put a deposit down on a future cruise while sailing on the current one, you can be eligible for discounts and onboard credit (i.e., free spending money for you). Get first-day discounts. Embarkation day can be chaotic. You’re getting familiar with the ship’s layout, signing up for all the things and likely going to the main dining room for dinner to meet your waiters. You might not even realize that the spa and specialty restaurants are open that evening. To lure passengers through their doors, onboard spas might offer first-day discounts and specialty restaurants might throw in a free bottle of wine. Book activities and packages in advance. Many cruise lines offer discounts for booking drink packages, Wi-Fi plans and shore excursions online before your cruise. It will save you money on your next cruise if you do some precruise planning instead of being spontaneous once on board. Go to the spa on port days. Most passengers get off the ship when it’s docked in port, so they prefer to book spa treatments on sea days. (The salon is especially busy on formal nights.) Cruise ship spas will often run specials or discounts to entice passengers to book treatments on port days, saving you money on the pricey massages and body treatments. Enjoy specialty restaurants at lunch. You can rack up quite the cruise bill dining at specialty restaurants each night of your cruise. To save money, look for extra-charge eateries that are open for lunch. The food is usually just as good, but the menu is smaller, and the prices are reduced from the dinnertime fee. Look for daily or happy hour drink specials. Your ship’s daily activity schedule (found in a printed newsletter or the cruise line's app) is your guide to saving money. Look for daily drink specials or happy hour deals that will save you money on those tropical drinks that are the hallmark of a Caribbean vacation. Or ask at your favorite onboard bar if they ever run drink deals, and plan your visits around those times. Book a drink or dinner package. If eating and drinking are how you spend your money on a cruise, you could save by bundling your purchases. Look for all-you-can-drink packages that will save you money if you plan to drink a lot each day or specialty dining packages that offer a discounted total price for booking multiple reservations in advance. Know when to skip the drink package. If you’re a casual drinker who doesn’t order more than a few drinks a day (including coffee and soda), or you don’t think you can drink enough to break even on the beverage package price every day, you will save more by skipping the package and ordering drinks a la carte, especially if you can utilize happy hour specials or loyalty perks to cut costs. Also note that NCL’s Unlimited Open Bar package that’s part of its Free at Sea booking promotion is not a truly complimentary perk; you’ll need to pay $28.50 to $32 per person, per day. If you typically don’t spend that much on cruise drinks, you’ll save more by going a la carte. Skip the souvenir glass. Step onto a cruise ship pool deck or atrium on the first day of your cruise, and you’re likely to be approached by a waiter offering you a drink in a souvenir glass. You want the cocktail, but do you really need to bring home a cup shaped like Carnival’s funnel? Say yes to the drink and no to the souvenir glass, and you will save a few bucks on the cost of the drink (not to mention the extra bag fees when you realize you can’t carry all those souvenirs home). Seek out free alcohol. If you pay attention, you can find several opportunities to get drinks for free on a cruise ship. Many of the onboard art auctions pass out Champagne or sparkling wine to attendees, and sometimes the ship’s shops will offer liquor tastings in an attempt to convince you to buy a bottle. If you’re a suite guest or loyalty member, you might be eligible for free drink vouchers, happy hours or events with comped drinks. Shop the sales for souvenirs. Cruise line boutiques often run BOGO sales or “everything for $10” hours on items like T-shirts, evening purses and sunglasses. If you’re thinking of purchasing some souvenirs, look for promotional events listed in your daily schedule. If you want to splurge on high-end jewelry or other expensive gifts, wait for those onboard shops to announce specials. These purchases won’t be cheap, but you might be able to save a bit or get an extra bauble thrown in for free. Check out the seminars. Your cruise ship’s spa or boutiques will often host seminars about wellness practices or understanding gemstones. These events are really marketing ploys to get you to sign up for spa treatments or buy shoe insoles or jewelry. However, they often convince people to attend by giving away spa credit or jewelry in a raffle. If you’ve got nothing better to do on a sea day, you might show up in the hopes of winning something. Spa tours and port shopping lectures also run raffles (plus, you might get a free massage for a minute). Look for midcruise specials. Cruise ships will discount paid attractions on the fly if they need to drum up more revenue in a certain area or if restaurants are not full. If you keep your schedule flexible, you can jump on midcruise specials, advertised in your daily schedule, and save on specialty dining, arcade games, spa treatments and more. Evaluate laundry costs. Doing laundry on board is a smart way to avoid checked bag fees by packing light. In some cases, sending a bag of laundry to be washed on board (especially if you take advantage of a midcruise laundry special) can be more economical than paying to check a bag. However, you can save even more if you take advantage of a ship’s self-serve launderette or hand wash small items in your cabin’s bathroom sink. Some top suites come with free or discounted laundry, and top-tier frequent cruisers might also get comped laundry as a loyalty perk, so check the options before packing as part of your savings strategy. Book your own tours. Cruise lines mark up shore excursions because they have to pay the provider and turn a profit. You can often save money by going to the source and booking a tour directly with a provider. Alternatively, a private tour guide for a group might not always save you money, but you will usually get more value out of a small-group tour that you can customize to your preference. Skip the tour and explore independently. You don’t need to shell out big bucks for an organized tour in every port. To keep costs down, skip the beach break tour and walk or take a bus or taxi to the beach. Do your own walking tour with a guidebook or app. Go on a hike or take yourself to a cathedral or museum. If you tour independently, you won’t have to pay for a guide or cruise line overhead. Look for less inclusive beach breaks. Sometimes a cruise line will offer several versions of the same resort day pass or beach break excursion — one that just covers your entrance and another that includes lunch and drinks and water toy use. If you don’t plan to eat or drink that much, or at all, you can save by booking the least expensive version of the tour and just paying for the amenities you use a la carte. Use local transportation. Taxi rides can add up quickly. Consider using less expensive forms of transportation to explore a city during your port stop. Local buses and subways can be more affordable ways to get around, plus offer a glimpse into local life. Use Wi-Fi in port. Cruise ship internet access is pricey; you might pay more for a week on board than you do for a month at home! If you don’t have to be connected at all hours, skip the cruise ship Wi-Fi plan and seek out free or cheap Wi-Fi in port. Many port terminals have free Wi-Fi, or you can grab a cup of coffee or a drink at an establishment in town with complimentary Wi-Fi for customers. Negotiate prices. Know when prices aren’t set in stone and negotiate a lower fee to save on your in-port purchases. You can often barter over the price of crafts, food or souvenirs in open-air markets, or negotiate rates for taxi tours or rides. Always be friendly and polite when haggling, and be prepared to walk if the vendor does not accept your offer. Bring your own beach gear. Most beaches you’ll visit on a cruise, including the cruise lines’ private islands, will rent you snorkel gear, umbrellas and beach floats, or sell you beach toys. Save money by purchasing and bringing your own snorkel gear, beach shade, inflatable beach toys and floats. The upfront cost might be higher than a single rental, but you can use the gear in multiple ports and on multiple cruises. Look for inflatables or collapsible gear that can pack down small or come in convenient carrying cases. Don’t eat lunch or dinner in port. I always recommend trying the local cuisine in port, both because it’s a fun way to experience a new culture and to support the local economy. But if you’re on a budget and need to cut costs, skip the meals in port and head back to the ship for meals in the many included eateries on board. Don’t forget to fill up on breakfast, so you can spend more time in port before hunger drives you back to the ship. If nothing else, avoid the overpriced and often inauthentic waterside tourist restaurants and ask around for where locals eat on the cheap — or skip the lunch and treat yourself to a cheaper gelato or pastry instead. You don’t have to employ every one of these tips to save money on your next sailing, but keep them in mind to make smart decisions as you plan your next vacation and once you’re on board. It’s always OK to splurge a little on vacation, but you want to make sure you’re not spending unnecessarily. What matters is that you’re getting the biggest benefit from your vacation buck. item.title: INSTRUCTION: Dubai and Oman on One Trip: Choosing a Visa That Lets You Come Back
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Dubai and Oman make an easy pair. Muscat is about an hour's flight away, the Hajar Mountains start just past the border, and many travelers fly into Dubai, spend a few days on the coast, cross to Oman, and return to Dubai for the flight home. On a map, it looks like one easy loop. On paper, it depends entirely on which UAE visa you hold, and the wrong one can leave you stuck on the Omani side. This is a practical guide to getting the visa right for a Dubai and Oman itinerary. American, British, and many European passport holders are currently stamped in at the airport without applying in advance, so each time they cross back into the country, they are processed at the border. For them, this question largely resolves itself, although it is still worth checking the current terms for your passport. Many other travelers need to arrange a UAE e-visa before they fly. If that is you, read on, because a Dubai and Oman trip is exactly the kind of plan where people buy the wrong visa. The standard UAE tourist visas for 14, 30, or 60 days are single entry. The moment you leave the UAE, whether by plane to Muscat or by road through a border post, the visa ends. It does not matter how many days were left on it. So a traveler who lands in Dubai on a 30-day single-entry visa, spends five days in Dubai, then crosses to Oman for a week, cannot use the same visa to return. They would need a new visa for the return leg, applied for and approved in time, with all the risk that brings at the end of a trip. A multiple entry visa is built for exactly this kind of trip. During its validity, you can fly out, drive out, come back, and repeat, with no limit on the number of crossings. Two details matter more than anything else. The clock starts on your first entry and never pauses. If you hold a 30-day multiple-entry visa and land on 10 November, the visa expires on 9 December. Days spent in Oman are not added back. Think of it as a fixed 30-day block on the calendar, not 30 days spent in the UAE. It cannot be extended. Your last flight out must leave before the block ends. Leave a day or two of margin in case a flight is delayed or canceled. There are two multiple-entry options: Count the whole trip from the day you first land in Dubai to the day you fly home, including time in Oman. If that total is comfortably under four weeks, the 30-day visa is enough. If it is longer, or your Oman plans are still loose, the 60-day visa is the safer buy. It is worth comparing the cost with the alternative. Two separate 30-day single-entry visas, one for each visit to Dubai, would cost $410 per person plus the stress of a second application while on the road. A Dubai multiple entry visa at $320 covers both visits on one PDF. If you are not leaving the UAE during the trip, skip multiple entries entirely. A single-entry visa does the same job for less. The route you take affects how much planning the crossing needs. By air. The simplest option. Flights from Dubai to Muscat are short and frequent, and you clear immigration as on any international flight. By bus. Public buses run between Dubai and Muscat. It is a long day on the road but cheap, and the desert and mountain scenery through the windows makes up for the hours. By car. Driving is popular, especially in the mountains. If you rent a car in the UAE, check before you book that the rental company allows it to be taken into Oman and that the insurance covers Oman. Many rental agreements do not. Expect a small exit fee when leaving the UAE by road. Musandam. The Omani peninsula north of Ras Al Khaimah is a separate trip, known for its fjord-like inlets and dhow trips. It is reached by road through a border post on the UAE side, so it counts as leaving the UAE like any other crossing. Your UAE visa only covers the UAE. Oman sets its own entry rules, and they depend on your nationality. Some passports can enter Oman without a visa for short stays, while others need an Omani e-visa before arriving. Check the Royal Oman Police e-visa site for your passport while you plan your route, not at the border. The documents are the same as those required for any UAE tourist visa. Scan your passport's photo page in color, and check that it has at least six months of validity. Add a current photo against a white background, the flight that takes you out of the UAE, and the address of your first night's stay. Nobody needs your whole route. The application only asks for the first landing and the last departure; whatever happens in between is your business. Allow three to four working days for approval. If time is short, get it in a day or a day and a half. Because the first entry must happen within 60 days of the issue date, applying a season ahead is a mistake. - Buying a single-entry visa because it is cheaper, then planning a trip to Oman in the middle. - Assuming the multiple entry clock resets each time you come back. - Booking the final flight home a day after the multiple-entry window closes. There is no extension. - Taking a rental car across the border without written permission from the rental company. - Remembering the UAE visa and forgetting to check Oman's rules for your passport. Here is how a two-and-a-half-week trip might work together. Land in Dubai on 1 February and spend five days in the city. Fly to Muscat on the 6th, spend a week in Oman driving through the mountains and down the coast, and fly back to Dubai on the 13th. Take two days at the beach, a day in Abu Dhabi, and fly home on the 17th. That is 17 days from first landing to last departure, with one exit and one return in the middle. A 30-day multiple-entry visa covers it, with nearly two weeks to spare. Get the visa right before you go, and the border becomes just another stop on the road. This story was published in partnership with eDubai Visa.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: BA's Best Lasagna
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it. Layers of slow-cooked pork-and-beef ragù, silky Parmesan béchamel, and pasta bake into a rich, creamy lasagna Bolognese with a browned top and crisp edges. Make the sauces ahead to break up the work, or settle in for a day of very good kitchen smells. The secret weapon is the meat sauce. Why make meatballs only to break them apart? Searing the meat in large balls leaves room for moisture to escape, so you get deep browning instead of a potful of steam. After a long, gentle braise, a potato masher turns them into ragù. Whole canned tomatoes, crushed by hand, give you control over the sauce’s chunky texture. One step you can skip: boiling the noodles. In side-by-side retests, regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil!) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. The ragù and béchamel provide enough moisture to cook the pasta in the oven—as long as every noodle is covered. Spread the sauces to the edges, leaving no dry patches, and making sure the sauce totally covers the top layer of noodles before baking. Round it out with homemade garlic bread and a Caesar salad. Do I need to buy no-boil lasagna noodles? No—use regular dried lasagna noodles, preferably De Cecco. Skipping the boiling step isn’t the same as using noodles labeled “no-boil.” In our original tests, those absorbed too much sauce, leaving the finished lasagna drier than we wanted. Why doesn’t this lasagna have ricotta or mozzarella? This is a lasagna Bolognese, built around meat ragù and Parmesan-enriched béchamel rather than a separate cheese filling. The béchamel supplies the creaminess, while Parmesan brings salty, nutty flavor. For a less involved version with a cheese filling, try our Cottage Cheese Lasagna. What’s the best way to split up the work? Make the ragù one day, then tackle the béchamel, assembly, and baking the next. For an even lighter second day, make both sauces ahead and refrigerate them separately; rewarm the béchamel just enough to loosen it before layering. The ragù can be refrigerated for up to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months, while the béchamel can be refrigerated for 1 day. Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app Saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna. Need to make a substitution? - Ragù BologneseStep 1Preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later). Step 2Warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done. Step 3Reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes. Step 4Add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours. Step 5Using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed. Do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months. - Béchamel and AssemblyStep 6Melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly. Step 7Preheat oven to 325°. Note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking. If parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper. Step 8Lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel. Note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel. Step 9Cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving. Do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking. Editor’s note: This recipe first appeared in our February 2018 issue as part of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. It has been updated with clearer assembly instructions and guidance from additional BA Test Kitchen testing, including the option to skip parboiling regular dried lasagna noodles. item.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh. The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap.
Cable cars and an Alpine zoo in Innsbruck, Austria When I got off the train in Innsbruck last December, its setting took my breath away immediately - dramatic mountain peaks soaring over the majestic imperial roofs of the city. The stunning golden dome of the town hall, glowing in the crisp morning sunshine, was another wonderful sight as I began exploring the cobbled streets of the old town. I stayed at the youth hostel right next to the River Inn, enjoying a lovely breakfast as the city woke up and the water rushed by, energising me to go out and enjoy the city. The Alpine Zoo is best explored in winter, with its native mountain creatures such as brown bears and ibex. The Nordkette cable car takes you up 2,000 metres in 30 minutes for great views and access to walks or skiing pistes. I used the Innsbruck Card (€79 for 48 hours) for free public transport and lots of discounts.
Bamberg in Germany casts a magical spell I first went to Bamberg in the summer – but a local pub owner told me it was much better in winter. How right he was. Last December, Bamberg greeted me in the guise of a gorgeous fairytale. Light snow dusted the medieval and baroque rooftops of the Unesco-listed old town, while soft mist rose like as if by magic from the Regnitz River around the pretty Little Venice area. The Altes Rathaus (town hall) looked as if was floating like a painting on ancient bridge, free from the weight of summer crowds. The central Maximiliansplatz lured me towards it in the evening as darkness descended, with the welcome warm glow of wooden stalls at the Bamberger Weihnachtsmarkt, filling the cold air with the scents of roasted almonds, gingerbread, and hot mulled wine. A trip up to Bamberg Cathedral was well worth it, offering wonderful views of the houses and forests around the city, making a perfect winter canvas day and night.
Medieval streets, waterways and soaring peaks in Annecy,France Annecy in Haute-Savoie, France, comes into its own in winter, with medieval streets hosting an array of beautiful cafes and shops, all surrounded by soaring mountains topped with snow. The winter sun reflects on the aquamarine lake while you dine on tartiflette or raclette. The area was controlled by Sardinia for centuries, giving it a unique atmosphere; the Savoyard flag is seen as often as the tricolor. For a longer stay, an early season day of skiing is easily accessible by bus. Cycle around the lake to the Chateau Menthon. It’s easy to get there from the UK by train.
Baltic beauty in abundance in Tallinn, Estonia Tallinn is a Baltic beauty that embraces winter with charm and panache. The cobbled streets of the old town, with its huge Christmas tree, horse-drawn taxis trotting along, candlelit cafes and snow-covered squares give the city a cool – in every sense – Christmas card quality. The city’s medieval walls are home to twisty lanes that are lined with spice-scented bakeries, medieval spires and secret cellars serving mulled wine with warming spicy salami. My breath frosted over as I walked up the Hellemann Tower, but it was worth it for the chance to walk along the 15th-century city walls for views over snow-dusted terracotta rooftops. I made good use of the Tallinn Card for €63 (for 48 hours) giving free entry to more than 50 museums and free public transport.
In Bergen, take the Fløibanen funicular from Bergen city centre up Mount Fløyen for spectacular views over the snow-dusted city, fjords and surrounding mountains. In winter it’s great to get there in the afternoon twilight in time for sunset to see Bergen’s lights come alive below. Afterwards, wander down toHanseatic Unesco site Bryggen for a warming coffee or hot chocolate.
Defy the winter winds of Leiden, the Netherlands While Amsterdam is the big cheese in these parts, Leiden, 30 minutes away, more than holds its own as far as charming cities of Holland are concerned. What’s more, it has a young, student vibe with not a whiff of dope anywhere. If you want canals, windmills, culture, good bars and restaurants, a great market with lots of vintage shops too, then Leiden oozes enough good hormones to envelope even the most jaded of travellers. In a lovely curved 1930s building, you can find Anne and Max for a gratifying and warming breakfast to get you going for the day. Strolling the streets of Leiden is like stepping into history when you consider that Rembrandt strutted his teenage genius around the place probably past the former Caecilia Hospital, now the excellent Rijksmuseum Boerhaave Museum. The vintage shops on Breestraat are perfect for very blissful and rewarding rummaging. The wind whips round those canals in winter like a razor blade, so remember to take the thermals!
Berlin in winter can be cold, wet and rather brutal looking. However, it also offers amazing museums, ample opportunities for hot drinks and cake to re-warm one’s heart and stomach, and attractive Christmas markets. Even better, a short train ride can take you out to one of the beautiful lakes that surround the city. A brisk stroll will blow any cobwebs away and then sausages and beer will provide the energy for the trip back into town. Berlin: scruffy, grey and probably bloody freezing, but always brilliant.
From our hotel in Prague, I followed the smell of roast chestnuts and baked gingerbread last December to the snow dusted streets of the old town. I quickly sensed that Prague embraces and enhances winter rather than fights against it. The Christmas market stalls were everywhere in its medieval streets and a towering tree in the Old Town Square was a joyful gathering place for families and friends. The Letná Masopust Carnival (held in late winter) was in full flow, featuring parades, theatre performances and stalls serving warming local treats such as smoked ham and spiced trdelník cake. I chanced on Golden Lane, a cool historic street of independent and vintage clothes shops. The Castle and Charles bridge are magically lit up and you can ice skate among the spires of Wenceslas Square.
Winning tip: pastel shades in the crisp air of Wrocław, Poland Wrocław is perfect for those looking for a winter city break beyond the main tourist trail. The city positively twinkles in the crisp air. Head over to Cathedral Island with its cobbled streets to watch the lighting of the gas street lights at dusk. Take a walk around the illuminated Market Square with its pastel-coloured buildings. Stay at the wonderfully restored art nouveau Hotel Monopol, the setting for Andrzej Wajda’s 1958 Ashes and Diamonds – a masterwork of Polish cinema.

item.title: IDEA: Beyond the Tourist Trail: Why Exploring New Destinations by Bike Is the Ultimate Travel Adventure
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
Travel is about discovering new places, experiencing different cultures, and building memories that last a lifetime. While planes, trains, and cars make it easier to reach popular destinations, there's something uniquely rewarding about exploring the world on two wheels. Cycling offers travelers a different perspective. Instead of rushing between tourist attractions, you can take your time, discover hidden destinations, connect with local communities, and experience landscapes more intimately. Whether you're riding through quiet countryside roads, exploring coastal towns, or discovering mountain trails, bicycle travel pairs adventure, freedom, and physical activity into one unforgettable experience. As cycling becomes an increasingly accessible travel option, finding the right bicycle has never been more important. Here's why exploring new destinations by bike might become your favorite way to travel. 1. Discover Hidden Places Most Tourists Never See One of the greatest advantages of bicycle travel is the freedom to explore beyond traditional tourist routes. When traveling by car or bus, you're often limited to established roads, scheduled stops, and popular attractions. Cycling lets you slow down and discover places that might otherwise pass unnoticed. Imagine riding through a quiet village, discovering a small family-owned café, or stopping beside a scenic viewpoint that isn't listed in most travel guides. These unexpected experiences often become the most memorable parts of a journey. Cycling encourages spontaneous exploration. You might discover a beautiful countryside road, a local market, or a peaceful lakeside path simply by taking a different route. For travelers who value authentic experiences, these small discoveries can be more rewarding than visiting crowded attractions. Travel tip: Use cycling-friendly navigation apps such as Komoot or Ride with GPS to explore quieter routes, and verify local access restrictions before heading onto unfamiliar trails. 2. Experience Destinations at Your Own Pace Modern travel can feel rushed. Packed itineraries, transportation schedules, and long lists of attractions often leave little time to truly appreciate a destination. Cycling changes this. Instead of moving quickly from one location to another, you experience the journey as such. You can stop whenever something catches your attention, take photographs, enjoy local food, or simply appreciate the surrounding landscape. Unlike hiking, cycling lets you cover longer distances while staying closer to your environment than you would inside a vehicle. For example, a leisurely coastal ride might take you past fishing villages, quiet beaches, local restaurants, and scenic viewpoints-all within a single day. The flexibility to explore at your own pace makes cycling particularly appealing to independent travelers. Travel tip: Avoid planning every minute of your cycling itinerary. Leave extra time for spontaneous stops, rest breaks, and unexpected discoveries. 3. Turn an Ordinary Holiday Into an Outdoor Adventure Not every memorable adventure requires traveling to a remote wilderness or climbing a mountain. Sometimes, a simple bicycle ride can transform an ordinary holiday into something exceptional. Mountain biking through forest trails, cycling along scenic coastal roads, or exploring countryside routes can add excitement and variety to any trip. The type of bicycle you choose depends on the terrain and experience you want. Mountain bikes are generally suited to rougher trails and off-road adventures, while road bikes work well for longer journeys on paved surfaces. Gravel bikes offer versatility for travelers who expect a mix of paved roads and unsealed routes. For travelers preparing for a cycling holiday, retailers such as BikesOnline offer different bicycle categories worth exploring, including mountain, road, and gravel bikes. Choosing the right bicycle can significantly affect comfort, handling, and enjoyment. However, the best adventure isn't necessarily the most difficult. A relaxed ride through a scenic destination can be as rewarding as tackling a challenging mountain trail. 4. Connect With Local Communities and Cultures One of the most meaningful aspects of travel is meeting people and experiencing cultures different from your own. Cycling naturally creates opportunities for these interactions. When traveling through smaller towns and villages, you're more likely to stop at neighborhood cafés, local markets, roadside food stalls, and independent shops. These encounters offer a more personal understanding of a destination. A conversation with a café owner might lead to a recommendation for a scenic route. A local cyclist might share information about a hidden viewpoint or a quiet road that doesn't appear in popular travel guides. Cycling lets you experience the rhythm of daily life. You see how communities interact, observe local traditions, and notice details easy to miss when traveling faster. For backpackers and independent travelers, these experiences often become highlights of the journey. Travel tip: Learn a few basic phrases in the local language, respect community customs, and ask permission before photographing people or private property. 5. Enjoy an Active and More Sustainable Way to Travel Cycling combines sightseeing with physical activity, making it appealing for travelers who want to stay active while visiting new destinations. Regular cycling supports cardiovascular fitness, muscular endurance, and general well-being. It also offers opportunities to spend time outdoors, which many travelers find refreshing after busy work schedules and long periods indoors. Another advantage is its low environmental impact. For local journeys, replacing motorized transportation with cycling can reduce emissions, especially when the bicycle is already available at the destination. The overall environmental impact of a cycling holiday varies according to factors such as flights, accommodation, equipment, and other transportation choices. Still, exploring a destination by bicycle can reduce reliance on motor vehicles during a trip. Travel tip: Combine cycling with trains or other public transportation where permitted to explore larger regions without needing a rental car. A common misconception about adventure travel is that it requires a large budget. Cycling trips can be adapted to a wide range of financial situations. You don't need to book an expensive guided tour or travel far to enjoy a memorable cycling experience. A weekend exploring nearby countryside routes, coastal roads, or national parks can provide plenty of adventure. Start by choosing a destination within a comfortable travel distance. Research cycling routes, accommodation options, weather conditions, and available facilities. If you're new to cycling, renting a bicycle at your destination may be a sensible option before purchasing your own. Travelers planning to invest in a bicycle can reduce initial costs by comparing models and shopping during seasonal promotions. For example, Black Friday bike deals can provide an opportunity to compare bicycles across different riding categories. Depending on the terrain you plan to explore, Black Friday sales can be a good opportunity to find discounts on mountain, gravel, and road bikes. Retailers such as BikesOnline and Reid Cycles are worth considering when researching bicycles for recreational riding and outdoor adventures. Beyond the sale price, consider factors such as comfort, quality, and how well a bicycle suits your riding style. A good deal is only worthwhile if the bike meets your needs. Before purchasing, consider bicycle fit, component quality, maintenance, warranty coverage, and suitability for your planned routes. A well-chosen bicycle can support many future outings, so long-term comfort and reliability matter more than a temporary discount. 7. Choose the Right Bicycle for Your Travel Style Not every bicycle suits every type of adventure. Before planning your trip, think about which destinations you want to explore and the surfaces you'll encounter. Mountain bikes are designed to handle uneven terrain, making them well suited for forest trails, rocky paths, and certain mountain routes. Their wider tires and terrain-focused designs can provide additional traction and control on challenging surfaces. They're particularly appealing to travelers who enjoy outdoor exploration beyond paved roads. Road bikes are generally designed for efficient riding on paved surfaces. They can be a good choice for travelers planning longer rides along coastal highways, countryside roads, or established cycling routes. However, riders should carefully consider traffic conditions and local bicycle infrastructure when planning road-based adventures. Gravel bikes have become a popular option for cyclists who want to explore mixed terrain. They can handle paved roads and unsealed surfaces, making them useful for routes that combine countryside lanes, gravel tracks, and longer-distance riding. For travelers who enjoy flexible itineraries, a gravel bike may offer a practical balance between efficient performance and versatility. Hybrid and Commuter Bikes for Casual Exploration Not every cycling holiday requires specialist equipment. Hybrid and commuter bicycles suit relaxed sightseeing, urban exploration, and recreational rides on smooth surfaces. Brands and retailers such as Reid Cycles offer options in everyday and recreational cycling categories that travelers can compare when planning less demanding adventures. The right choice ultimately depends on comfort, terrain, trip duration, and personal preference. 8. Essential Tips for Planning Your First Bicycle Travel Adventure A successful cycling adventure requires preparation, especially when exploring unfamiliar destinations. Here are a few practical steps to make your journey safer and more enjoyable. Research your route. Look for established cycling paths, quieter roads, and trails suitable for your experience level. Check whether bicycles are allowed on your chosen route. Check the weather. Strong winds, heavy rain, extreme temperatures, and sudden changes can affect cycling conditions. Plan accordingly and avoid unsafe situations. Pack essential equipment. Bring a properly fitted helmet, water, basic repair tools, a spare tube or puncture repair kit, lights, and weather-appropriate clothing. Understand local cycling laws. Helmet requirements, road rules, lighting regulations, and trail restrictions vary by destination. Plan your accommodation. If you're traveling for several days, look for accommodation with secure bicycle storage and convenient access to your planned routes. Know your limits. Choose realistic daily distances based on your fitness, terrain, elevation, and weather. Include recovery time. Prepare a backup plan. Know how to access public transportation, emergency assistance, or bicycle repair services if something goes wrong. For international cycling adventures, check whether your travel insurance covers your activities, especially mountain biking or other higher-risk cycling experiences. Good preparation allows you to spend less time worrying about logistics and more time enjoying the journey. 9. Create Memories Beyond Traditional Sightseeing Some of the most memorable travel experiences happen when you move beyond well-known routines. Cycling encourages curiosity and exploration. You might start your day with a simple route in mind, then discover an unexpected viewpoint, a charming village, or a beautiful stretch of countryside along the way. Unlike tightly scheduled sightseeing tours, bicycle travel creates space for these moments. It also provides a sense of accomplishment. Completing a challenging route, reaching a scenic destination, or finding your way through an unfamiliar area can make the experience rewarding. Memories often extend beyond the places you visit. You remember the people you met, the food you discovered, the challenges you overcame, and the freedom of exploring somewhere new alone. These experiences can turn a simple holiday into a lasting personal story. Final Thoughts: Your Next Adventure Could Begin on Two Wheels Exploring new destinations by bicycle offers what traditional travel doesn't always provide: the freedom to slow down, discover unexpected places, and connect more closely with the world around you. Whether you're cycling through scenic countryside, exploring coastal towns, or discovering mountain trails, every journey presents opportunities for adventure and personal discovery. You don't need to be an experienced cyclist or own expensive equipment to start. Begin with a manageable route, choose a bicycle suited to your needs, and gradually expand your adventures as your confidence grows. The world is filled with incredible destinations waiting to be explored, and sometimes the most memorable experiences happen beyond the usual tourist trail. So, wherever your next journey takes you, consider experiencing it on two wheels. The adventure might be closer than you think. This story was published in partnership with BikesOnline.

item.title: Where was The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping filmed?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping filmed? We’re heading back to Panem for the sixth time this autumn, as the latest Hunger Games prequel hits screens. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the action of the first film, and tells the origin story of Katniss Everdeen’s grumpy tutor, Haymitch Abernathy, as he enters the Hunger Games himself. Based on the books by Suzanne Collins, the dystopian series is set in a futuristic America in which each ‘district’ must send a teenage tribute to fight to the death in an annual competition – the idea being that by doing so, the public will be too afraid to rebel against President Snow. This edition of the games is known as the ‘Quarter Quell’, with double the number of tributes being sent into the arena – meaning the stakes are so much higher. Interest in the film is high, not least because Haymitch is such a popular character from the original series, in which he was played by Woody Harrelson. Newcomer Joseph Zada takes the lead role in this latest film, while Hollywood heavyweights Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning and Kieran Culkin also star. One of the most important sets in the film is the arena where the games take place, and for this, director Francis Lawrence opted not for CGI and a green screen, but instead a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in northern Spain. Here, we look into the locations used in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping ahead of its release on 17 November. Where was The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping filmed? Within the book and film series, the settings for the Hunger Games are always known to be virtually spectacular. For this film, filmmakers settled on the vast and untouched landscape of Somiedo Natural Park in the Asturias region of northern Spain, which boasts mountain ranges, glacial valleys, beautiful meadows, dense forests and tranquil lakes. The remote region is also home to the last brown bear population in Europe. When the tributes are launched into the arena, they are presented with a vast Cornucopia, a pile of weapons, food and other supplies that might be useful to them in the competition. These scenes were filmed at Somiedo Natural Park, with the Asturian mountains and a glacial lake in the background. “Somiedo is a spectacular place,” supervising location manager Pedro Aráez shared. “The valleys, forests and mountains have a very wild, untouched feeling, which was exactly what the filmmakers were looking for. It’s remote, dramatic and visually unique. When you arrive there, you immediately understand why it was chosen.” The Teverga beech forest, located close to Someido, was used for some of the dense woodland scenes, in which contestants battle it out and hide in the woods. Other scenes filmed here utilised a series of glacial lakes, the Saliencia Lakes and the Lago de la Cueva. Before the tributes are launched into the arena, they are first held in special little pods underground which are arranged in a circle around the Cornucopia. The perfect location for this? A Velodrome, of course, which is famously circular so the cyclists can race round and round it. The film crew utilised Berlin’s Velodrom for this very purpose, with its cold, clinical silver decor perfect for matching the high-tech aesthetic associated with the Capitol. Prior to entering the Games, the tributes must first ‘introduce’ themselves on the public stage, during a televised Grand Chariot Parade in the Capitol. Another Berlin location with links to the sporting world was used for this purpose – the Olympiastadion Berlin. For fans of the earlier films, this is the moment when Jennifer Lawrence’s character Katniss becomes ‘the girl on fire’ with her incredible flaming dress. The futuristic architecture of the Calatrava Building in Oviedo, Spain, with its white claw-like structure, stands in for a building in the Capitol, where President Snow and his government live. Designed by Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, his work is known for resembling living organisms. The 14th-century Ehreshovens Castle just outside of Cologne was also used as a filming location, with local press reporting that its lush interiors might have been used to stand in for somewhere inside the Capitol. A former smelting factory complex in western Germany, Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord, provides the backdrop for one of the most atmospheric settings in the films, Haymitch’s home of District 12. The vast complex is able to stand in for multiple places within the district, which is known for being a former mining town that has fallen on seriously bad times. Rather than being a desolate area stumbled upon by the filmmakers, Landschaftspark is popular with locals, who come here to see the nightly light installation by British artist Jonathan Park. There are also regular al fresco events here, including not only film screenings, but also the Ruhr Games (which blends sports and arts) and the Traumzeit Music Festival. Another location in Germany, Lindlar Quarry, was also used for District 12, with wooden huts built here to resemble the outskirts of the village.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Cheaper rides, double miles: How to save on your Thanksgiving trip to the airport
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The busy Thanksgiving travel season is just about to kick off as millions take flight around the country. You can expect crowded terminals, long security lines and potentially surge-priced rides to and from the airport. The good news is that major ride-hailing players Uber, Lyft and Blacklane all have launched Thanksgiving offers, including one that is exclusive to our TPG members. Here's how to make the most of your holiday ride transport. Through Nov. 30, Uber is running a promotion called "From Bad Seats to Better Rides." If you get squeezed into a middle seat with no armrest or end up in the last row by the lavatory, you could receive up to 30% off your Uber ride home from the airport. To take part, register your flight and seat details on Uber's Thanksgiving promotion page. Uber provides several examples of undesirable seats but has not published a complete list of what qualifies as undesirable. Individual savings vary, and terms apply, so check the offer added to your Uber account before booking. In our testing, you will not be required to submit a boarding pass or an image of your undesirable seat to receive a discount. TPG tip: Link your Delta SkyMiles and Uber accounts and select Delta as your earning partner before you travel. item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion. In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks. To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later). If you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream. Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well. For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste. With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities. - Use a bigger bowl than you think you need. Remember: Cream roughly doubles in volume when you whip it and can easily slosh out of a too-small bowl. - Keep things cold. While you certainly could start with room-temperature equipment, we recommend putting your bowl and whisk or beaters in the freezer for 10–15 minutes first. Use straight-from-the-fridge cream too. Chilling the equipment isn’t essential, but it helps your whipped cream come together faster. - Add any sugar or simple flavorings. If you’re making sweetened or vanilla whipped cream, add the sugar, vanilla extract, or other simple flavorings to the cream before you start whipping. That gives the sugar time to dissolve and distributes everything evenly. - Start whisking. Whisk vigorously, moving around the bowl and lifting the cream as you go. A side-to-side motion, rather than making circles around the bowl, is most effective. You’ll know you’re on the right track when the whisk starts leaving trails in the cream. - Stop when you reach the texture you want. Soft, medium, and stiff peaks all have their place; more on how to tell them apart below. Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding. But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping. If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir. Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping. You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped. Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch. Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple. Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie. But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert. How to make whipped cream without a mixer There’s more than one way to whip. By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want. In a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount. Secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking. Can you make whipped cream ahead? Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert. You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes. Need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours. For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape. In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet. If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound. This is probably a temperature issue. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.
