Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes. If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out. Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter. Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with new reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

item.title: IDEA: I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand. The view is a welcome excuse to catch my breath before continuing along five more rolling cliffs—400 steep feet up, 400 steep feet down, and repeat. And so, despite my exhausted legs and the blister that’s forming over my right big toe, I decide to imprint this impossibly peaceful scene into my brain to remind myself why I’m doing this trip. I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes. Earlier this year, it became part of the newly created King Charles III England Coast Path, inaugurated with a brisk March walk by the king himself (wearing a suit, natch). The route now incorporates all of England’s preexisting regional coastal paths, adding new sections to create a wider network that stretches across nearly 2,700 miles, giving walkers a chance to access parts of the country far beyond the typical travel itinerary. Since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths. I realized I could experience so much more of the country’s most beautiful landscapes by foot than I ever could by train or car. For my second foray, I chose one of the more frequented set of trails: walking east from Weymouth to Bournemouth across Dorset. This stretch is known for its incredible rock formations, the result of millions of years of waves washing against the coast. That erosion has also led to the discovery of some of the world’s oldest fossils—giving the region the name of Jurassic Coast. When I’d set off five hours earlier from the charming seaside town of Weymouth—a destination made popular by King George III’s multiple visits at the turn of the 19th century—the going had been easy. My only roadblock was a military parade that a British historical society couldn’t have arranged any better: an Army band marched in front of a stretch of beach-facing Georgian townhouses as Union Jack bunting fluttered in the sea breeze. An Anglican priest delivered a short prayer. There was a Spitfire flyover. If you ignored all the iPhones and mobility scooters, it was a scene that would have fit in comfortably 80 years ago. By setting out alone on a three-day walk, I was seeking solitude, and moments like that clifftop break, when I had the view all to myself, delivered. But the long way out of the Weymouth hubbub also clarified why walking England’s coastal paths is so approachable—especially for those of us who love the outdoors but want to sleep indoors. Since the country is quite densely populated, you can easily walk the trails from town to town, and hotel to hotel, without the weight (and stress) of camping equipment. For those same reasons, it’s also perfect as a solo walker; the risks feel more manageable when you know medical care is within reach; that you’re rarely without phone service; and that your hotel door locks at night. After 12 miles or so of walking, I arrived at West Lulworth, a town of centuries-old stone cottages that can best be described as “quaint.” I was greeted by the famous Durdle Door, a limestone arch that snakes out of a cliff and into the Channel, with clusters of beachgoers splashing underneath. It's a place worth lingering: After going down my final descent of the day, I snuck a peek at Lulworth Cove, a popular bay almost fully enclosed by limestone (and a UNESCO World Heritage Site), before checking into the Old Barn Inn, a B&B up the road for a gloriously hot shower. My second day of walking presented a new challenge: Part of my planned route was closed because it crossed a firing range in use by the Army for training. To avoid it, I rode the bus (the Jurassic Coast is very well served by public transit, at least in summer) part of the way to my next destination, then planned to take a shortcut through some fields to get back to the coast. Sarah, the owner of the Old Barn, had given me extremely specific verbal directions based on local landmarks, which were easy enough to follow until I’d reached the “horrible hill” she warned me of. It was then that I realized I was in the middle of a field with no obvious path out. I bushwhacked to a nearby road, the peace of solitude nowhere to be found as I muttered, “I’ve done this to myself.” But thanks to my two puny bars of cell phone service, I navigated over another field, through a herd of sheep, along a ravine, and then emerged, alarmingly sweaty, into the absolutely charming limestone village of Worth Matravers. I made a beeline to the local pub (as recommended by Sarah), and enjoyed what was undoubtedly the best pint of my life looking out over a grassy field—and to the ocean beyond. As I sipped my lager at a picnic table, a forceful summer wind whipped off the water, knocking down the pub’s sandwich board advertising Cornish pasties, but it didn’t bother me or the handful of other pubgoers sitting out in the sun. Perhaps there is something to the old saying about victory being sweetest after you’ve known defeat, because for all of the frustration I endured that day, the second half of my walk was absolutely breathtaking. After an easy, peaceful meander back down to the coastal path, I spent the next two hours walking through clifftop fields where I saw more deer and cows than humans, and past the famous Danding Ledge, a stone shelf jutting into a patch of sea popular with wild swimming enthusiasts. The wind that had teased me earlier died down closer to the water, and all I could hear was the crash of the waves against the rocks below. When I’ve needed a moment of peace in the few months since then, I’ve summoned the memory of that afternoon and the calm those clifftop fields offered. I woke up the following morning in the seaside town of Swanage with calves so sore that the thought of any incline made me nervous. To my dismay, I discovered right away that, to pick up the coastal path from the inn where I’d stayed (Rivendell Guest House), I first had to climb a steep staircase from the sandy beach, up the cliff to the bluff. Thankfully, shortly thereafter things flattened out. It was also the busiest section of the trail I encountered—though, even here, I saw only a dozen or so people, mostly locals in athletic gear out for a morning ramble. When I reached the hilltop, I was greeted by a few hundred cows—and just beyond their enclosure, the Old Harry Rocks came into view. Millions of years’ worth of waves have chiseled away at this promontory, carving a series of chalk stacks that now sit away from the mainland. I watched two ambitious kayakers appear on the side of the rocks where the water was calmer and stare up at the feat of nature—enjoying a perspective that I’m sure is heavily advised against, and which only few have gotten to enjoy. The final part of my walk was along Studland Beach, a sandy four-mile stretch that backs up onto a nature preserve. I waded into the water, sat in the sun, and saw a boat selling ice cream delight children up and down the crowded beach, before reaching the last mile—which also happens to be home to the UK’s most popular naturist (or nudist) beach. The ice cream boat pulled up again, and it tickled me to see that the evenly tanned sexagenarians were just as pleased to have a midday treat as the energetic children I'd just passed. The final adventure of my trip also brought out childish delight in me: To get to Bournemouth, where I’d catch a train back to London, I had to take a four-minute ferry ride. Alongside me on the ferry was a double-decker bus with its upper deck open to the elements, letting passengers take full advantage of the beach breeze. The sheer logistics of this was a thrill to witness: a convertible bus driving onto a boat. On the other side of the strait, I got onto that very bus—aptly called The Breezer—and watched as the natural coastline was slowly enveloped by an urban milieu. It was a slightly rude awakening to reemerge into Bournemouth, a small university city where the asphalt had soaked up the sun, presaging the upcoming heatwave. But I realized as I walked through the train station that I was inadvertently grinning with pride. I assumed no one would ask me, a stinky and visibly sweaty woman, what I’d been up to, but if they had, I would have been all too happy to tell them about my solo walk along the South West Coast Path.

item.title: This popular London park could get a new outdoor swimming pool for the first time in nearly 40 years
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Londoners love an outdoor swimming pool. From the much-loved Tooting Bec Lido and London Fields Lido to the dreamy ponds in Hampstead Heath, the capital has plenty of spots for a refreshing dip when temperatures rise. And now, another outdoor swimming destination could be on the horizon, as plans to bring back a historic East London lido have taken a major step forward. Victoria Park, one of East London's best-known green spaces, could welcome a brand-new outdoor swimming pool, almost four decades after its original lido closed. On Thursday 12 November, Tower Hamlets Council approved a budget of up to £2.5 million for a specialist design team to assess the feasibility of building a new lido in the park, develop initial designs and prepare a planning application. The project is part of a pledge made by Lutfur Rahman's Aspire party ahead of the local elections in May 2026. The park's original lido first opened on 16 May 1936 and became one of London's most popular outdoor swimming spots. During the Second World War, it was used to supply water to allotments in the park before being damaged by an incendiary bomb. It reopened in 1952 following extensive repairs, but suffered further damage during the Great Storm of 1987. The pool eventually closed in 1989 and was demolished the following year, with the former site now occupied by a car park and an open space known as Lido Field. Now, almost 40 years later, the council hopes to bring outdoor swimming back to the park. The proposed development could include a heated outdoor pool, changing facilities, family-friendly spaces and community wellbeing facilities, with the possibility of year-round use. Cllr Minara Khatun, Cabinet Member for Leisure, Culture and Tourism, said: “A new lido at Victoria Park could become a fantastic asset for the borough, helping people of all ages and backgrounds to enjoy the physical and mental health benefits of outdoor swimming while supporting wider community wellbeing.” The exact location has yet to be decided, and the design team will assess several potential sites within the park, taking into account accessibility, affordability, environmental sustainability and the surrounding historic landscape. The project is also intended to address a shortage of swimming facilities in Tower Hamlets. According to the council, residents currently make more than 12,000 swimming visits outside the borough each week because of limited local capacity. But when could Londoners actually take a dip? If everything goes according to plan, a planning application could be submitted in September 2027. Subject to approval, construction could begin in early 2028, with the council aiming for a summer 2029 opening. However, the project remains subject to further approvals, funding and feasibility assessments.

item.title: IDEA: Is there any food that can’t be improved by a bun?
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink
Is there any food that can’t be improved by a bun? Tim Hayward conducts three very scientific experiments to find out what happens when you turn some of the world’s most elaborate dishes into sandwiches Like any group of obsessives, food lovers enjoy nothing more than a good argument. It’s probably because we lack any rounded knowledge that might enhance conversation. Like music fans, wine enthusiasts and, for all I know, train spotters, we hotly defend entirely spurious origin myths. You know the sort: “Before Elizabeth David discovered it, you could only buy olive oil in Boots for cleaning your ears,” or “The Earl of Sandwich, seated at the gaming table in his club, was the first to consider slapping something between two bits of bread.” We also love a doctrinal debate with all our congested hearts: “If a pie doesn’t have a pastry bottom, is it just a lidded stew?” Or, “Is a hamburger a sandwich?” It keeps us happily entertained for hours, or at least until the main course arrives. Mostly this is harmless. While Samuel Pepys was burying his “parmazan cheese” in his back garden, fellow diarist of the Great Fire John Evelyn was expounding the virtues of “oil of Lucca” in the dressing of “salletts”. Working people have been putting bread and cheese together pretty much since the invention of both. If God can exist in three hypostases that are coeternal and consubstantial through a shared homoousion, then cannot a pie be a pie in two sacred forms? And, as for the hamburger, that’s a quantum thing. It is, and it isn’t a sandwich, but you only know which if you open the box. But what one might call The Sandwich Complexity is a broader problem and bears some examination. The origin stories of both the sandwich and the burger centre on the idea of convenience. The hamburger served in bread is attributed severally to Americans “Hamburger Charlie” Nagreen, Frank and Charles Menches and Fletcher “Old Dave” Davis, who all offered patties in buns at various fairs at the turn of the 19th century so customers wouldn’t require plates. For most of history, the sandwich has been subordinate to a meal. Something to be consumed quickly and away from the correct space of restaurant or dining room. Today, you can be served any number of highly curated sandwiches in a sit-down environment and expect to pay a great deal for the privilege. Surely it can’t be true that the definition of a sandwich is merely “something made convenient to eat through the medium of bread”? It’s a compelling thesis, but if we follow it down, then first a doner kebab is a sandwich, then a smørrebrød is a sandwich, at which point we are forced to acknowledge that a folded slice of pizza is a sandwich — and then the centre cannot hold and anarchy is loosed upon the world. We’re losing our grip on what a sandwich actually is. So, I resolved to experiment. First, I listed my favourite proper restaurant dishes. Dishes that require cutlery, napery, fine china and staff to cook and serve them. The stuff you need a bank loan to buy and a trolley to get to your table. Then I planned to stick them in a bun. To make a sandwich of each. Would this ruin the dish? Might it improve it? More importantly, would it be a sandwich? I began with the purely theoretical. I seemed to remember Italian sandwich shops, back when such things existed in London, used to do a hot Wiener schnitzel in a soft Italian roll. I could add a fried egg to that, a few anchovies and capers and we’d have veal Holstein in sandwich format. That looked pretty good on paper. Then I served vitello tonnato at a dinner party and had the leftovers in a sourdough baguette for lunch the following day. That was a very promising development. And so began the practical trials in earnest. Experiment 1 : BEC “Arnold Bennett” The BEC, or Bacon, Egg & Cheese, appears on grill counters all over America and Canada, a quick-to-eat construction, almost as old and distinguished as the hamburger. It combines bacon with yellow plastic cheese product and either a runny fried egg or, more commonly, an omelette. The omelette created at the Savoy in 1929 for the novelist Arnold Bennett is an absurdly rich combination of smoked haddock in a cream-enriched béchamel, topped with cheese. It is one of the great dishes of British cuisine, and a personal favourite. What if the two met? Could a BEC-Arnold actually work? You’d usually buy a BEC in a Kaiser roll. These are fun to make if you’re a breadhead, but aren’t common in British bakeries, so substitute a large floury bap, stottie or Scottish morning roll. Don’t be tempted by brioche or anything with an enriched dough — it quarrels with the filling. A large English muffin also works (and looks amusingly like an Egg McMuffin when served). QuantityIngredients200g milk Bay leaf200g undyed smoked haddock25g plain flour25g butter, plus more for frying 5g Dijon mustard75g fresh grated parmesan2 eggs1 soft roll Bring the milk to a low simmer. Then add the bay leaf and the fish. Remove from the heat immediately, cover and leave for 10 minutes. Lift out the fish. Remove the skin and try to keep the fillet together. The fish will want to flake, but you want to find substantial chunks in the finished dish. In a separate pot, cook the flour in the butter to make a roux, then strain in the poaching liquid and whisk to create a thick sauce. Remove from the heat, stir in the mustard and half of the cheese and check the seasoning. In a small bowl, beat and season the eggs. You’ll now need your largest frying pan. An Arnold Bennett is a deep, soft omelette that should be constrained in a small pan, but a BEC needs a thin, wide one that allows the egg to wrap around the filling. Put a knob of butter into the hot pan, wait for it to foam then pour in the beaten eggs and swirl around to cover the surface. As soon as the egg starts to set, place the fish in the centre. Pour over half the sauce and sprinkle on the remaining cheese. Use a spatula to fold the edges of the omelette back over the filling on each side to create a closed egg envelope, which you then turn over to seal and continue to warm through. Split the bun and fry the cut face in any butter remaining in the pan. Lift the package into the bun, pour over the remaining sauce and consume immediately, preferably standing at the stove. Is it good? Utterly. Is it better than an omelette Arnold Bennett eaten with a knife and fork? Absolutely. Is it still a sandwich? Affirmative. Good so far. Let us proceed. Experiment 2: Lobster roll “À la Newberg” This is the bastard child of Lobster Newberg, the more refined antecedent of the Thermidor, and the cheery dockside lobster roll. The Newberg — lobster meat cooked in a sauce made with butter, cream, egg yolks and sherry — is said to have been created in 1870 at Delmonico’s in New York, for a sea captain called Ben Wenberg. (I know, this is turning into another of those barking-mad origin tales.) Wenberg is supposed to have fallen out with Charles Delmonico, who banished him from the restaurant, then anagrammed the dish and kept it on the menu. If you believe any of that, I have a crypto investment scheme you might be interested in. Lobster Newberg delights me because it’s one of the great classics of table-side theatricals — a recipe performed by a waiter with a chafing dish and a cold, hard eye for a substantial tip. It has an excellent pedigree. QuantityIngredients1 batch-baked hotdog roll50g butter 1 lobster tail (defrost if frozen)10g medium-dry sherry10g brandy150g cream2 large egg yolks, beaten Freshly grated nutmeg and cayenne to taste First, fry the torn sides of the roll in butter. Remove the meat from the lobster tail and cut into 1cm-thick chunks. Sauté the lobster in butter and deglaze with the sherry and brandy. These are the two main flavouring components, so cook off the alcohol but don’t reduce all the way or take more than two minutes. While it’s still short of cooked, remove the meat, leaving a load of butter flavoured with lobster and, of course, booze. Add the cream and reduce it while you beat the egg yolks in a separate bowl. This next bit is called tempering, and it can be the most terrifyingly cheffy thing ever, but do not be afraid. Take the reduced cream off the heat, then spoon a little into the bowl of yolks while whisking. Repeat this twice. In the old days you’d have done this next bit in a double boiler, but today we have thermometers. The cream will cool, so when it reaches 80C, pour in the egg and cream mixture while vigorously whisking. You’re basically making a runny savoury custard. Turn the heat back on and jockey things carefully to stay between 80C and 84C. The idea is to thicken the sauce without scrambling the eggs (eggs scramble at 85C). Split your roll. As soon as the sauce thickens, add the lobster meat and an extra dash of brandy, plus nutmeg, cayenne, salt and pepper. Once it’s fully warmed through, spoon the meat into the bread and pour over the sauce. Is it good? A catastrophic understatement. Better than Newberg with a knife and fork? The sauce trickles down your chin. Of course it’s better. Is it a sandwich? Controversial. The filling is added downwards into the split roll, so it is questionable whether it’s strictly between bread or merely on it. A nuanced point. But if we say it is a sandwich, we might have to accept that a hot dog is a sandwich too, and I don’t think I can go that far. In which a pared-back Tournedos Rossini — beef fillet topped with foie gras and Madeira sauce — meets a bun. The night before you plan to cook, season the beef with salt, wrap the bacon around its perimeter and tie in place or pin with a toothpick. Then leave uncovered on a cooling rack in the fridge. This dries the outside of the meat, making it easier to sear. QuantityIngredients1 brioche burger bun. For maximum irony, find one with sesame seeds5g tomato purée1 500g pouch of ready-to-use liquid beef stock1 20clcan punchy red — a Côte du Rhône or a Malbec Butter1 slice of beef fillet, 3cm thick, 10cm in diameter1 rasher unsmoked, streaky bacon1 trimmed and cleaned chicken liver100g Madeira Slice the bun in half. I normally wouldn’t give house room to brioche burger buns — a pointless gilding for an already delicious lily — but researching recipes for tournedos I noticed that half of them seemed to suggest serving on brioche toast. This would also be consistent with the huge tranche of foie gras that’s usually balanced on top of the meat in the classic presentation. I confess I baulked at foie gras. The idea of searing it has always made me feel uncomfortable. It is, basically, a rich and delicate concentration of fat that degrades the second it hits the hot pan. It’s morally complicated enough just spreading it on toast, but to purposely damage it with heat seems casual and profligate. In this case, I feel better off with a chicken liver. Many of the flavours are still there, only more robust and better able to stand up against Madeira sauce, a high-octane Booze Gravy. Put the tomato purée into the bottom of a saucepan and cook it through, about a minute on medium heat. Pour over the stock and simmer to reduce by half, then add the red wine and reduce by half again. Before anyone howls, this isn’t a proper demi-glace, but it’s a quick, field-expedient sauce base. Heat some butter in a frying pan and sear the tied meat for two and a half minutes on either side. Roll the cylinder back and forth on its side for another minute or so to cook the bacon. If you have a probe thermometer, remove from the heat at 52C core temperature. It will rise to 54C while resting. Once the meat is resting, sear the chicken liver. We’ve become quite keen on the idea of chicken livers remaining rare at the core, but they are a wonderful breeding ground for campylobacter, so good sense suggests they should be cooked to a core temp above 70C. In this recipe, there’s plenty of rich liquid around, so the liver won’t be dry. Now, deglaze the pan with the Madeira, and once it’s lost the initial, highly winey smell, spoon in some of the sauce base. Adjust the seasoning, including a splash more Madeira if you like the booziness. It would not be wrong to whisk in a little butter either to make the sauce glossy. Sear the cut faces of the bun in a dry hot pan. There’s enough butter, sugar and egg in brioche for it to brown and crisp quickly. Mash the chicken liver on to the bottom of the bun. Top with the beef (check any string or toothpick has been removed) and drench it in sauce. Perch the lid on like a Maga cap on an elephant seal. Is it good? Yes. Emphatically. Is it better than Tournedos Rossini with a knife and fork? Hell yes. Is it a sandwich? Almost certainly. And if it isn’t, it’s a hamburger. Is there anything that can’t be improved by putting it in a bun? I have found nothing so far – well, except trifle, but I’d had a lot to drink. I vow to continue the research programme and am now actively seeking funding. My DMs are open. Find out about our latest stories first — follow FT Weekend Magazine on X and FT Weekend on Instagram

item.title: IDEA: I Baked My Way Through The Atlantic’s Archives
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. The most cherished recipes are usually the hardest to follow. They live on stained index cards and notes worn thin at the creases, in handwriting so faded you have to squint to read it. That handwriting belongs to a grandmother or a distant relative, and it was meant for someone who already knew the dish: Add a pinch of this, a teacup of that; bake until done. I’ve spent a lot of time in The Atlantic’s archives, and I kept running into such recipes tucked into letters, essays, and memoirs, rarely where you’d expect them. I was curious to know whether they still work—and, more important, how they taste. The further back I went, the less my finds looked like recipes. They read like stories, and you had to read closely to find the instructions. Take this “Letter to a Young Housekeeper,” from November 1865, written by C. P. Hawes to “M.,” a bride newly married to “H.” Hawes spends most of the letter arguing that cooking is a fine art and a science, which the woman of the house should learn for herself. She is funny about it, and a little grand. Recalling one early success at the table, Hawes reaches for Henry David Thoreau, whose essays had recently run in this magazine, to describe the dishes: “We ate, lingered, and revelled in them, thus becoming epicures at once … They were as great a revelation to the palate as Bettine or Thoreau might be to the mind.” Only at the very end does she mention a “well-tested” recipe for bread: a quart of milk, a teacup of “hopyeast,” and enough flour “to make it quite stiff.” How much flour? How hot an oven? And how long does it bake for? Hawes doesn’t say. For much of history, recipes moved from one cook to another by word of mouth and by experience: watching a mother at the stove, having a neighbor ask for a missing ingredient. Cookbooks didn’t exist simply because, for centuries, most women couldn’t read, Sarah Lohman, a culinary historian, told me. As literacy spread in the 18th century, women began keeping handwritten notes of family recipes to pass down or to copy for a daughter when she was married. Those recipes were light on instructions by design. They expected you to rely on your instincts “to know when the batter looks right or to know when the cake is done,” Lohman said. By the early 20th century, written recipes had become something to amass, and cookbooks were treated as literature. “It was with something of a shock that I woke one morning and found myself a collector of cookery books,” the American writer Elizabeth Robins Pennell wrote in The Atlantic in 1901. What she prized most were the traces that earlier owners of the books left behind. Her copy of The Queen-Like Closet, a 17th-century cookbook by Hannah Woolley, had several owners before it reached her—one of whom was a young woman named Mary Halfpenny, who had received it as a gift in 1678 and went on to add her own recipes to its pages. A century later, another family used it as their “Bible,” recording their children’s births in the margins. Pennell loved those scribbles: “They add a distinctly personal charm to the shabby little old cookery book.” And sometimes, the actual Bible held recipes too. In 1910, a writer in this magazine’s Contributors’ Club described the family Bible as a place where you might find anything tucked between the pages, from a father’s old report cards “to mother’s recipe for sponge-cake.” But around midcentury, the American recipe changed shape, in part due to technology. I asked Lohman why some of the 19th-century recipes I’d baked didn’t call for butter or eggs. Before the advent of the refrigerator, Lohman explained, these ingredients were seasonal: Cows give milk after calving, from late winter into summer, and hens tend to take a break from laying in winter. Sure enough, the 19th-century recipes missing those ingredients were fall and winter dishes. By the mid-1950s, the majority of American homes had a refrigerator. As kitchens changed, recipes changed with them: more exact, more complete, easier for a stranger to follow. But the story behind the food has never quite gone away. Even as recipes grew more precise and the ingredients in them stopped shifting with the seasons, the people who wrote them kept reaching for memories. In 1985, Corby Kummer, then an editor at The Atlantic, began an essay on pie not with flour or butter but with a tale about his mother’s pie crust, an unforgettable taste that “has driven me to pursue the elusive art of making pastry.” And as recipes moved online, the stories came with them. Food blogs, and later videos, wrapped their instructions in anecdotes; anyone who has looked up a recipe on their phone knows the feeling of scrolling past several paragraphs of backstory before the ingredient list appears. Some of that is less sentimental than it seems (long blocks of text help a recipe rank higher in search results and make more room for ads). Still, it is telling that when food writers have space to fill, they fill it with stories. I have been baking since I was a child, learning from my mother and grandmothers and from recipes handed down for generations. I was curious whether the recipes I found from over the decades still hold up today. So I baked my way through the archives, beginning with Hawes’s 1865 biscuits and ending on a batch of brownies from 2010. Where an ingredient or instruction was missing, I filled in what I thought each recipe left out and made my best guess about certain directions (what it means to age in a tin, or to roll to “exactly the right thickness”). The recipes below are adapted from the originals, based on my own testing (I’ve indicated any discrepancies with the original recipes by adding “modified” to the ingredients list). Here’s what happened—and my honest assessment of how it all tasted. In C. P. Hawes’s Atlantic story, she promises her dough will make “two small loaves and a half-dozen biscuits.” What came out of my oven were plain dinner rolls, and only about a dozen (there was no dough left for the loaves). Today’s biscuits are made with butter; Hawes’s dough is mostly milk, flour, and yeast. And not the yeast we buy now. Home bakers used to make their own, often by brewing it with hops. Hawes calls for a teacup of this so-called hop yeast—I used a packet of active dry yeast instead. The result: a simple bread roll with a slightly floury taste. Not quite a Thoreau-level revelation. But if you want a very simple dinner roll for the table, this is the recipe for you. (And if you’re after a tall, fluffy biscuit, Amanda Mull cracked the code in 2018.) Lutes gives no quantities at all—she just writes that the dish needs a deep bed of sliced, spiced, buttered apples under a thick crust, baked “at least an hour, very slowly.” The result: a slightly watery dessert that isn’t the prettiest, but tastes decent. The consistency of the filling needed improvement, and it also could have used more flavor (I’d recommend going heavier on the spice). The result: This one was divisive among my taste-testers. The Lebkuchen is dense and very chewy, a workout for your jaw too. But if you like something not too sweet or soft to dunk in tea, this could be your cookie. The result: Kummer’s crust was so good that it stood out to the people who tried it. (Store-bought just doesn’t compare to his recipe.) The filling was a big step up from Lutes’s Dowdy. Emanuel himself says his filling is “almost identical to the one for apple pie,” and that’s how it tasted: like a solid, classic apple pie. Overall, a satisfying combination of recipes. The result: very good brownies with a perfect texture that were not hard to make. They were a favorite with my tasters. Definitely worth baking a batch. Family recipes are still finding their way into the pages of The Atlantic. For the December issue, Danyel Smith wrote about her Aunt Louise’s famous mac and cheese and the unexpected ingredient that set it apart. Does your family have a recipe like that, with a secret, a story, and one person who makes it best? I’d love to hear about it. Let us know in the comments. (We may share your answer, including your first name and last initial, age, and/or location, with fellow readers in a future edition of this newsletter or on our website or social-media platforms.)

item.title: REVIEW: Review: Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX Winter Hiking Boots
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
The Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a new waterproof and insulated hiking boot from Oboz, known for its popular 400g Bridger 10″ and 200g Bridger 8″ insulated mid winter hiking boots. Modeled after cross-country ski boots, the Katabatic Storm GTX is a lightly insulated mid-height boot insulated with aerogel-based Solarcore bonded to a Gore-Tex liner, providing waterproofing and warmth without added bulk. The result is an active winter boot with about 80% of the warmth of Oboz 200g insulated Bridger boots, that’s robust enough for use with lite traction aids like Kahtoola Microspikes or Hillsound Trail Crampons. - Gender: Men’s (women’s available) - Weight: 18.5 oz per shoe in a men’s 10.5 - Insulation: Aerogel bonded to Gore-Tex If you’re a hiker, but you don’t hike in winter, you’re missing out on a lot of fun. Gone are the bugs, roots, and rocks that can make three-season hiking unpleasant. The trails are less crowded, and there are lots of new skills to learn and gear to play with. In the past 15 years, winter footwear has gotten lighter and lighter due to advances in insulation technology, material science, and manufacturing practices. The introduction of lightweight traction aids, like microspikes, was a real inflection point because they could be used with footwear that has lightweight, flexible soles, requiring no special training like rigid mountaineering boots and crampons. Several companies, including La Sportiva, Hoka, and Salomon, have attempted to introduce lightweight mids and trail runners for winter use with mixed success, because there are so many different types of winter hiking outings, from trail running and snowshoeing to light mountaineering, all targeting different user types, temperature ranges, complementary gear types, and trail conditions. With that in mind, the Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a winter hiking boot, not a trail-running shoe, because its sole is too rigid. It is lightly insulated, with about 80% of the insulation of a 200g Thinsulate boot, and is good for temperatures down to about 15 degrees as long as you are moving and not standing still. It has enough front toe-kick rigidity to work with traction aids like Kahtoola Microspikes or Hillsound Trail Crampons without causing friction on top of the toes, which can lead to blisters or cold toes because of reduced circulation. The boots have a gaiter hook, making the boots compatible with gaiters. The outsole has lugs that provide good traction on snow and frozen slush when you’re not wearing a traction aid. Fitwise, the Katabatic Storm is true to size. That said, they’re patterned on cross-country ski boots, with a quick-lace system and a zippered top cover, which makes them a little time-consuming to put on and hard to adjust if you use an articulated lacing technique that requires different pressure at different points along the lacing track. I’m not a huge fan of either, but they fit me well enough, hold my foot securely, and don’t cause any hot spots inside. I was a little leery of the Katabatic Storm GTX when I learned they only have a warmth value of about 80% of a 200g insulated winter hiking boot. The insulation they do have is only located in targeted areas such as underfoot, over the toe, and through the tongue, but not along the sides and around the heel. The shoe is designed for movement and managing the heat it generates, but not for standing around. Why would that be an issue? As a winter hiker, I generally recommend buying insulated boots that will keep your feet warm when you’re not moving and are standing still. This is especially true if you hike in the backcountry where you may have to wait a long time, say 8 hours or more, for search and rescue to come and help your injured hiking partner while you wait with them, or if you have to slowly walk an injured hiker out into the wee hours of the morning. That’s not the time to wear a lightly insulated boot designed only for movement. That might sound overly conservative, but I have participated in backcountry winter rescues that ran into the early hours of the following day, and we were all very glad we were wearing heavily insulated boots. The insulated Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX boot is lightweight and comfortable, even on challenging hikes that require traction. I just wish they were available with more insulation that’s equivalent to the 400g Oboz 10″ Bridger insulated winter hiking boots I wear today. If they were, I’d wear them on every winter hike. As such, they’re ideal for shoulder season weather and spring conditions where there’s ice and slush on trails, but temperatures are warmer during the day. Because they are only lightly insulated, I reserve them for winter hikes on warmer days and close to accessible trailheads where local SAR crews can muster and arrive relatively quickly in an emergency. Disclaimer: Oboz donated boots for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides.

item.title: The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging. Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye. Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar. There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time. “We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said. Ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert. After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions. “That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee says. Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily. Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus. “We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.” For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards. “We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu. Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood. The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions. “I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he says. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”

item.title: A Hiker Fell off a Cliff in Big Bend National Park. Then Rescuers Had to Leave Him There Overnight.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Big Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city (Photo: National Guard) A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Big Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48. According to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders. Rescuers reached the area just after 9 P.M. and called the Georgia Army National Guard medical evacuation crew assigned to the Joint Task Force-Southern Border. The organization works with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor the shared border between Texas and Mexico, an area central to a heated national debate over the Trump Administration’s border wall construction. The helicopter crew had taken off, but with limited lighting and winds approaching 35 miles per hour, and a string of storms moving into the area, the Black Hawk medevac crew made the difficult decision to scrub the mission. “The crew agreed it was not safe and we had to make the unfortunate decision to go back and try again in the daylight,” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Gregory Hiett, the aircraft commander, said in a statement. “It was an extremely difficult thing to do, knowing the patient was going to be stuck out there for the rest of the night.” Throughout the night, park responders remained on-scene and on the ground. Just after 9 A.M. on November 14, a second helicopter mission launched with a hoist rescue team. Flight medic and technician Holly Johnson descended 150 feet on a cable, determined the hiker was uninjured, and secured him in a rescue vest into the aircraft. The mission was finished by 10:45 A.M., and the hiker was transferred to Big Bend Regional Medical Center. “During a complex hoist operation in rugged, inaccessible terrain, our medevac crew successfully reached and evacuated an injured hiker when no ground rescue option existed, delivering the patient safely to higher medical care,” Lt. Col. Teresa Parrotta, commander of the 29th Combat Aviation Brigade, Maryland Army National Guard, said in a statement. Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Big Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city. It’s rugged, isolated, and enormous, spanning 800,000 acres with sheer 1,500-foot limestone cliffs. The National Park Service warns visitors to expect unreliable cell service, sparse infrastructure, and primitive roads—conditions compounded by the intense Chihuahuan Desert sandwiched between the Chisos Mountains. Reaching a hiking trailhead is challenging because roads frequently wash out from flash flooding, and many backcountry trails require high-clearance, four-wheel-drive vehicles.

item.title: On Tour: Australian Indie Darling Radio Free Alice on Tour Life, Guerrilla Gigs, and American Motels
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
This article is part of a new series, On Tour, in which we talk to touring artists about life on the road. On Halloween, a bouncing crowd of skateboarders, witches, ghosts, and ghouls slowly coalesced in New York City's Tompkins Square Park. They were there for a quintessentially East Village pop-up concert headlined by the Melbourne-based post-punk band Radio Free Alice (followed by an after party at Niagara). The band's debut album, What’s In Between, was just released the day prior, blending the high energy of ’80s new wave with biting social satire and a healthy dose of cheek. Having picked up a following in Australia and Europe, the four-piece group has built an underground reputation on guerrilla gigs like this one—held everywhere from beneath London railway bridges and Melbourne’s former Pentridge Prison to suburban backyards in Austin, Texas. That’s what makes the album title so apt: The young Aussies are caught between cities and countries, trying to make sense of everyday life while the road itself starts to feel like home. They’re in the thick of their own coming-of-age story, and one that's unfolding on an international stage. Fresh off the first dates of a nearly sold-out European lineup, tickets are now on sale for their What's In Between North America tour, which will kick off in San Francisco on February 24, 2027. Earlier this month, vocalist and guitarist Noah Learmonth picked up my call from a Sprinter van somewhere in Germany, on the road from Copenhagen to Berlin. With the wit, gumption, and on-stage vocals of a Gen-Z Morrissey, his devilish grin fills the screen as he tells me he spends 99% of his time in the window seat behind the van’s little table, facing forward. His preferred seat is currently occupied by guitarist Jules Paradiso. He gives me a 360-degree tour of their ecosystem, where everyone has settled into their own version of life on the road. Drummer Lochie Dowd has claimed a small sleeping nook near the back. Michael Phillips, bassist and resident reader, sits with his Kindle, having just finished Christos Tsiolkas’s The Slap. As for who’s running the show? “Fuck, no one,” the still-grinning Noah says. “There’s a man up front called Ben, our tour manager, who’s a crazy man. He’s the one who leads the blind. We’d all be fucked otherwise.” What’s everyone’s travel personality on tour? Who’s running the show? Yeah, [I'm] type D. I’m sort of in my own world when I’m traveling—headphones on, that kind of vibe. Jules is really easy company. He’s a valuable asset to have in the world. Michael’s pretty chill, too. He’s looking at me now as I summarize his personality. Lochie likes to sleep in this little nook. That’s a big part of his tour experience: finding that little nook. When we met Ben, we just fell in love with him and his crazy methods, his madness. The thing about Ben is he gets our sound right every time. It’s really annoying when someone else does the sound and you watch the videos back and go, ‘Oh my God, what the fuck? Why is there no bass in the synth? Why do we sound like Duran Duran? What’s going on? I sound like Sonic Youth.’ That’s not at all what we were going for. Two of my favorite bands, though. But Ben gets exactly the sound we’re going for, and he’s a real empath. We’ve spent so much time on the road together. He’s our guy. Where do you stay while you're on the road? When we’re touring Europe, we’ll stay in budget hotels. Either an Ibis or a Travelodge. In America, it’s more motel-type places—Motel 6 kind of things. It’s very cliché, but kind of sick in a way. Each morning when you wake up, you set your alarm for half an hour before you have to leave, get up, have a shower, smash your clothes into your backpack, and run down to the lobby so you’re not late and Ben doesn’t give you a verbal spanking. What's the food situation? Terrible. I just had McDonald’s. I don’t even like McDonald’s. You literally don’t have an option. You pull into a service station and the only food there is McDonald’s. Jules is a Big Mac guy, though. I know that. What are your packing styles? I’m personally notoriously light. I just have this yellow North Face backpack that I’ve had since I was about seven years old. My auntie gave it to me for my birthday. My trusty yellow backpack. Lochie has a big suitcase, Michael has a smaller suitcase, and Jules has a big, backpacker-style backpack. Essentials you can’t tour without? I’m wearing the same jeans I’ve been wearing every day for the past year. I got them from a thrift shop in Melbourne. So my essentials are my jeans. Lochie’s are his headphones—we all use Sony. Jules’s is…video games. He’d hate that I just said that. Let’s say his laptop. Michael’s is his Kindle. He’s the best reader. Let’s see what he’s reading…ah, he just finished The Slap. What's your favorite city that you've played in so far? New York. I mean, the obvious answer is New York. New York’s the best city in the fucking world. It’s amazing. The first few times we were there, we partied a lot. We just said, ‘This is a fucking adult amusement park.’ It’s ridiculous. We were staying with this band called Been Stellar, too, who are great. When we’re back we like going out on the Lower East Side, especially to this bar called Treasure Club. I personally also love the diners. I think the atmosphere in an old-school, family-run diner might be the best atmosphere of any place in the world. Favorite venue you’ve ever played? A gig is just people playing music, and it can happen literally anywhere. There are no rules. You can do it anywhere. Shaking up the gig setting—rethinking what a gig is and what it can feel like—is really fun, and it keeps it important. The Melbourne set at Pentridge Prison [a former 19th century prison that's been transformed into a residential area] was sick. It was an incredible visual. What about a city that surprised you? Zurich. So random. I just remember having a strangely amazing time. I remember leaving that gig thinking, ‘Actually, there was something incredibly awesome and sweet about that.’ And it was the people. They were just these thoughtful, sweet people. After a show like Zurich, we’ll be in the green room after. We’ll probably crack open a beer, and Lochie will be funny. If it went really, really well, we might go out somewhere nearby, to a pub or a bar or something. But generally, what happens is we go back to the green room, we’re really buzzed, we’ll have a beer and we’ll be pretty hyped up. Then Ben will come in and say, ‘All hands on deck. We need to load up the van. We’ve got to get to the next city.’ Zurich, though—I’d love to do it again. What's your impression of the United States so far? I mean, there’s one thing about America: the difference between, say, New York and LA, and then LA and Minneapolis or somewhere, is worlds apart. You could be in completely different countries. Middle America can feel like an absolute time warp. When you’re on the road, there’s a sort of repetitiveness to the long stretches of road that all seem to look exactly the same. You arrive at a petrol station that’s identical to the last one you stopped at. There’s that stereotype that Americans are big talkers, but I’ve found that’s almost underrated. I can’t believe how chatty Americans are. They love just talking, going on and on. Coming from Australia, it’s the opposite. I love it. Any memories you've made on the road that you’ll never forget? The first time we played in LA, this very sweet girl called Alice randomly made us all these gifts. She gave us all these handmade things: embroidered bracelets with band-related names and glasses with our names on them. I find something quite American about that. It’s just so sweet. In Europe, people tend to be a little less expressive in that way. It’s still just amazing to me. Which city has the best crowd? Glasgow had this sort of “rara”-ness to it, which was really fun and funny for us. It just felt so boisterous. We’d play a slower song, and they’d still find a way to just absolutely lose their minds. It was cute. When you're not on tour, where’s home for you guys? Nowhere, not really anywhere. I’m not exaggerating. I feel disingenuous calling anywhere our home at this point. But if there were one, it would be London. It’s making a big impression on us. What’s cool is that, a year before we moved to London, we played to maybe one person at one of our gigs there. Then, the following year, we played to this really big, sold-out room. It was an incredibly high-energy, adrenaline-fueled, amazing, crazy show. That was special. I’ll never forget it. It was probably my favorite show. There are so many young indie-rock bands coming up in London that I’m seeing, and they’re all ambitious and exciting. I’m really excited by London. It’s lived up to the hopes I had for it. Because of that we’ve found ourselves hanging out at venues like the Shacklewell Arms and the George Tavern, that sort of thing. While you're on tour, what do you miss the most? You know, this isn’t a very cool answer, and I kind of wish it were, but the truth is I really miss having an exercise routine. In Melbourne, I was really big on swimming every morning, doing laps or going to the gym. I find it puts me in a really good place for the day. I’m chill and focused, not neurotic, and I just find it’s really good for me. What's a band touring right now that you are personally excited about? Lime Garden. They’re an all female lineup. The English rock scene is a bit of a sausage fest, so they’re a breath of fresh air.

item.title: IDEA: The most beautiful winter day trips from London for a magical escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I am a self-proclaimed city girl. I cannot imagine living anywhere else but in a big city like London, with its infinite number of things to do, new corners to discover, vast array of restaurants and cafes to use as a refuge from the cold and an electric atmosphere that is hard to reproduce in quieter corners of the country. But even urban lovers like myself sometimes need to breathe some fresh air, and a good winter day trip from London strikes the perfect balance. Once I moved to the UK, my first ever trip away from London was to the Midlands. At the time, I was told it was sometimes described as a rather unglamorous weekend getaway from the city compared with more polished locations like the Cotswolds, but I remember loving the vast, green expanses of the English countryside, the horses running in the fields and the small farm shops – so much so that I even pondered the idea of finding a piece of land in the vicinity. I’m not sure what my plan was with this piece of land I had in mind – a private camping patch, perhaps? – but although I never ended up buying a little corner of Leicestershire, I kept the promise I made to myself to explore as much of the country as possible, even if it was just one weekend at a time. After a few years spent between trains and road trips, these are my favourite winter day trips from London.

item.title: REVIEW: 9 Best Coffee Subscriptions, Reviewed & Reordered (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
There’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans. That’s where coffee subscriptions come in. But the best services will do more than guarantee you’ll have a consistent supply of freshly roasted coffee—they also let you explore the vast world of coffee. They’re how I’ve discovered some of my favorite roasters, tried single-origins I never would have found on my own, and figured out exactly what I like and don’t like in a cup. Whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a new craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you. After five years of testing, Trade is our top pick—but depending on what kind of coffee you like, I have plenty of other recommendations. - The best coffee subscription service overall: Trade - A globe-trotting, single-origin subscription: Atlas Coffee Club - Award-winning coffees from a variety of roasters: Podium Coffee Club Platinum - The freshest, most flavorful coffee subscription: Origin Roasted - A text-to-order service for exciting coffee on demand: Fellow Drops I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers. To date, we’ve tested nearly two dozen options and recommend the following wholeheartedly. New in this update: BA editors have been trying out some new deliveries, including some we’re loving from Methodical in Greenville, SC, and Fellow’s Drops program. The best coffee subscription service overall: Trade Trade is a multi-roaster subscription that sources coffee from independent roasters all over the country. It's great for someone looking for great specialty coffee with an interest in trying a number of different roasters and different roasting styles. This was the easiest subscription I have ever set up, and Trade did such a good job of hitting my preferences right in their sweet spot: medium roast, medium body, medium fruit…just medium all around. I have gotten stuck in the past, tasting the same coffees or coffee styles over and over, and after just two bags, I could tell this would be different. I set up an order for one 12-oz. bag of whole beans every two weeks. The first bag was Atomic Roasters Space Cadet out of Peabody, MA, and my second bag was Sparrows Coffee, Harmony Series All Seasons Blend from Grand Rapids, MI. I loved the Sparrows bag because it had just enough roast to feel pleasantly dense and weighty on my palate, yet with enough fruit, brightness, and acid to feel lively. When I clicked the box for “medium roast” coffee, this is exactly what I had in mind. I only do pour-over at home, and this was awesome in my Hario V60 coffee dripper. Recently, senior shopping editor Olivia Tarantino tried Rarities, Trade’s newest program. It’s invite-only, with a rotating lineup of coffees that roasters make as experiments or passion projects. Each coffee is roasted and shipped to order, in batches of a few hundred bags at most. Trade provides detailed instructions direct from the roaster about how to best prepare your beans to get the optimal flavor extraction. She enjoyed an extended fermentation Chiroso variety that had complex acidity of citrus fruits and a slight savory flavor. We haven’t seen anything like Rarities from a subscription service, so serious coffee drinkers should jump on it. The bottom line: There is a lot of great coffee in the world, but finding it and getting it right when you want it can be a challenge. Trade takes care of that for you, making this subscription absolutely worth it. - A generalized service that partners with over 50 roasters - Very intuitive interface and flexible ordering options - Complete trackability so you know when more coffee is coming If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used. Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one. The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable. The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers. - Variety of coffees you never would have heard of or tried - Cool and unique flavor notes and/or experimental processing For the globally curious coffee connoisseur: Atlas Coffee Club If you’re a curious coffee connoisseur looking to try single-origin coffee from around the world while directly supporting fair trade and sustainable practices, Atlas is the subscription service for you. Every month, you’ll get a bag of single-origin coffee from a different country that comes with an ID card detailing sourcing information and tasting notes. Tester: Kelly Janke, former director of culinary production The ordering process was easy. It asked me a few questions about my preferences in roast level, brewing type, and coffee quantity, with options ranging from a half bag to four bags per month. The shipping did seem to take longer than I expected, which was my main qualm with the service. The beans I received in my first month were medium roast from Rwanda. I really enjoyed the cards that came in the box with tasting notes and information on the growing region. I had chosen two bags per month because I drink a fair amount of coffee, but it’s worth noting that this meant I received two of the same exact coffee (which wasn’t clear at the time of ordering—I had assumed they would be different). I ground the beans in my Oxo burr coffee grinder to a medium grind and brewed them in a Chemex with a metal reusable filter using a 1:16 coffee-to-water ratio. The coffee definitely tasted on the darker side of a medium with notes of grape, red apple, and roasted almonds. The bottom line: I love to try new coffee varieties and appreciate the difference; if you feel similarly, then Atlas is a great option for you. - Cost is reasonable, considering it’s fair traded, sustainable, and globally sourced - Thoughtful packaging and information cards - For the double bag option, would like to be able to opt to receive two different coffees The best decaf coffee subscription: Swiss Water If you’ve been reading all of this as a decaf drinker, we have good news for you: there are also some great decaf coffee subscriptions out there, including Swiss Water. This subscription offers a rotating selection of decaf coffees from roasters all across the US, all of which have gone through the Swiss Water process, a chemical-free decaffeination technique that you can read more about here. Note that Swiss Water currently only offers whole bean coffees, so you’ll need to grind your own beans if you decide to try it out. I opted for biweekly shipments, though Swiss Water also offers weekly, monthly, and bimonthly. The first coffee I received was from Manzanita Roasting Company, based in San Diego. There was no informational card included, so all I really gathered about the coffee was that it was from Guatemala and had notes of berries and chocolate, which it did. For a decaf brew, I was impressed by the quality and nuance of the flavor. The same can be said for the second bag of beans I received, which was a blend called Kick Back from South Carolina–based Barista Alley. The bottom line: You won’t find the kind of customization and curation options here that you see in most of the other subscriptions on this list, but if you’re okay with trying out a range of decaf coffees and aren’t married to one particular roast level or flavor profile, this service will work for you. - Great quality decaf coffees from a wide range of roasters - Shipment dates can vary depending on roasters’ timelines For the freshest, most flavorful coffee money can buy: Origin Roasted Of every coffee subscription we’ve ever tried, this one is unique. Most coffee beans, even if freshly roasted, are stored as green beans for months. Origin Roasted beans hit the roaster almost immediately after harvest and get shipped out right after that. Truly, they are the freshest coffee beans you can get without picking them yourself. It’s a subjective call as to whether that makes the flavor "better," but it makes it different. Fruity or chocolate tasting notes that are present in beans that sit green are massively accentuated with Origin Roasted beans. If a flavorful cup of coffee is what you’re after, these beans are as flavorful as they come. The brand’s commitment to roasting at the beans’ origin has the added effect of bringing more coffee roasting work and expertise to countries of origin; roasting for most American coffees happens in the United States. The ordering process is straightforward because there are no choices for you to make. Just give them your address and credit card number, and the coffee will be on its way to you at the end of each month. The company only sends the beans it is harvesting that month, which come from a single farm somewhere in Central or South America. The locations are limited to ensure that Origin Roasted can actually get the beans to your door while they’re as fresh as they’re supposed to be. I got beans from all over Central and South America: Guatemala, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Peru, and Brazil. Each coffee was entirely unlike the one that came before it. Shipments only get sent out on the 28th of every month, so I was limited to one bag per month. The bottom line: Because of the harvest and roast process, this really is a boutique product, so you can’t order en masse the way you can with larger roasters. I don’t think it makes sense to identify my favorite beans here because you, dear reader, are not guaranteed to get them anyway. What you are guaranteed to get are incredibly cool coffees. - Flavors that are bigger and unlike any other subscription - Guaranteed coffee that is “in season” - Can’t give any input on what coffee you receive The coffees brewing in BA editors’ kitchens right now We are always on the hunt for roasters and subscriptions we haven’t tried. These are the ones that have landed in our grinders recently that we’re loving. If you're into the idea of coffee drinking as a ritualistic ~experience~, Folk Coffee Club is for you. Founded by a Q-Grader, a.k.a. a sommelier for the coffee world, Folk specializes in rare coffees that score at least 86 points (in Q-Grader speak). Unlike many of the other coffee subscriptions on this list, Folk gives you zero options; instead, they'll send you one shipment every month with two expert-curated coffees. What really sets Folk apart, though, are the intentional extras they included with each shipment. Along with the two coffees, each month features a piece of art, a curated playlist, some thought starters, and a tasting guide that elevate the mundane ritual of coffee brewing and drinking into a full-blown experience you're encouraged to slow down and savor. The whole package, coffees included, is meant to draw on a unifying theme. Folk's first shipment, Volume 00, was titled “Off Script,” and featured two Gesha coffees—a distinctive varietal that takes supreme care to grow. Each coffee tasted unlike any other I've had, one with notes of jasmine and caramelized peach, the other reminiscent of blood orange and dark chocolate. The whole thing was beautifully packaged and felt like a luxurious gift to receive, the thoughtful intention behind each component highly evident. The bottom line: Think of Folk like a monthly ritual, complete with art, a playlist, and rare coffees you won't find anywhere else. If you're the type to linger over your morning cup, this one's worth every penny. - Must receive 2 coffees, monthly—no flexibility when it comes to frequency There is no better proof point that the world of exquisitely roasted coffee beans has anchored itself absolutely everywhere than the Onyx Coffee Lab. Onyx was started by Jon and Andrea Allen (who would later become a U.S. barista champion) in Springdale, Arkansas, in the Ozarks, and as it has spread throughout the state, it has also become one of the most recognizable names in specialty coffee. Such is Onyx’s reputation that it’s bled over into other areas, landing the Rogers, Arkansas headquarters a nod as a James Beard Award finalist for the best bar program in America. As for the coffee subscriptions themselves, they’re straightforward to set up: simply tick the box for quantity and the box for frequency. Onyx offers the reliable roaster’s choice option with a lot of interesting single origins and one-offs (I particularly liked a Rwandan washed coffee from Kanzu Station) that all include the most informative explainers I’ve ever seen attached to a bag of coffee. The cards include a breakdown of all the inputs that contribute to the cost, detailed brewing instructions for both pour-over and espresso, and an explanation of the fermentation and roasting process. For people looking for more familiar flavors, Onyx has subscription options that combine a small amount of more adventurous beans like the Kanzu with its more familiar blends, letting curious drinkers dip their toes in something new. And for a more special experience, Onyx releases a small number of memberships to what it calls “Echelon” for monthly deliveries of its rarest coffee. - Options for both adventurous and classic coffee drinkers - Lots of fun nerdy info included with each coffee Fellow’s coffee program is different than anything else we’re recommending here because it’s on demand and text-based. Sign up for Drops and every week you’ll receive a text with access to a hard-to-get coffee from a variety of roasters from all over the world. I’ve been signed up for the texts for about a year and I’ve gotten coffee from some of the better-known American roasters (the Onyxs and Equators of the world) as well as getting exposed to cool projects out of Denmark, Japan, and Australia. Every drop includes a detailed description of where the coffee comes from and what it will taste like. Ordering is simple. When you sign up, you’ll load your address and payment method into your account, so you simply reply to the text with the number of bags you want and a few days later they’ll be at your door. The Greenville, South Carolina roaster has grown now to have five cafes, a robust bakery and tea program, and some of the coolest, most beautiful branding in the coffee world. But it also has a wide range of blends and single-producer beans. I first walked into Methodical’s café in Greenville in 2017 for a single origin pour-over, and at the time quick national shipping of fresh coffee was still in its early stages, so that stop didn’t end with me signing up for regular deliveries. But now the infrastructure is there and the coffee is great. Methodical sorts its coffee into three main buckets for three different types of coffee drinkers: classic (where you’ll find medium and dark roasts great for batch brewing and espresso), contemporary (where you’ll find medium roast coffees great for batch brewing or pour-over), and “avant-garde” (where you’ll find lighter roast coffees, sometimes fruity, sometimes tea-like, that are best enjoyed black). How we tested the best subscription coffee services Our editors have used every one of these coffee subscriptions in their homes over several months and some for years. We’ve made sure to try a variety of bean types where possible, and to try the beans with a variety of brewing methods to see how well they perform as espresso, pour-over, drip coffee, and French-pressed coffee. Our editors are continually testing many of these services and constantly trying new coffee subscriptions to keep this list updated as the market changes, so be sure to check back as we update it often. What makes a good coffee subscription service There are hundreds of coffee subscriptions out there, so we followed two guiding principles when selecting which subscriptions to test: A coffee’s freshness has a huge impact on its flavor once brewed, no matter if you’re using a fancy espresso machine or a simple French press. The best subscription services will guarantee freshly roasted beans, either roasted to order or within a week or so of shipping. The other major factor in your coffee’s flavor is how recently the beans were ground. I’m a big advocate of ordering whole-bean coffee and grinding the beans just before brewing, so all of the options we tested offer that. (Of course, I know that many people may prefer the convenience of ground coffee. Most of the services below also offer that as an option, although my colleagues and I will continue to raise our eyebrows at you until you get a good coffee grinder.) Other coffee subscriptions we’ve tried and liked Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor Best for: People who want high-quality coffee, but aren’t interested in choosing from a dizzying array of adventurous options Intelligentsia, out of Chicago, is one of the OG players in third-wave coffee (if you’re unfamiliar, "third wave" has a specific meaning, but is sometimes used as shorthand for a generation of coffee roasters deeply invested in quality, consistency, and unique flavors in coffee). Intelligentsia’s House Blend and Black Cat espresso roast have become staples at bakeries and coffee shops all over the country, and its subscription service gives you a regular supply of those two as well as its deeper catalog of different beans. There’s one single origin option, but the subscription itself is mostly based around Intelligentsia’s blends, which rotate seasonally. This is a pretty simple, straightforward subscription. There is no quiz or process to determine what kind of coffee is “best for you”; rather, you just manually put in which subscription you want, choosing between the same blend (including espresso), rotating blends, or the roaster’s choice. You can also select how many times a month you want beans and how many bags you want per shipment. Changing to a different subscription is also quite easy. While you won’t find the same kind of personalized curation options as some of the other subscriptions on this list, Intelligentsia does offer one of the widest ranges of grind types if you aren’t getting whole bean coffee, running from the finest Turkish coffee grind to a super coarse (even coarser than cold brew) percolator grind. I got “Intelligentsia's Choice” because I’m a sucker for single-origin beans (and have had the opportunity to try all their classic blends already). The beans came from some of the strongholds of international coffee production: Ethiopia and Nicaragua. Making a carafe of pour-over coffee a day, enough for two people or one me, I used about one bag every two weeks. The most noteworthy coffee to me was a very fruity natural process Ethiopian coffee. After testing it extensively, I can tell you that this is a reliable, relatively affordable subscription; the Intelligentsia Classics subscription is only $17 a bag. It would be worthwhile for anyone who wants quality but isn’t trying to be too adventurous with their morning coffee. Just to note, in 2015, Peet’s bought up a majority stake in Intelligentsia.
